en.title: Bleeding After Menopause: Why It Always Needs Checking
en.excerpt: Any bleeding after twelve months without a period needs checking, however light. What the appointment involves, and why every episode counts.

children.text: Once you have gone twelve months without a period, any bleeding at all should be checked promptly — including a single spot, a pink smear, brown discharge, or one episode that stops on its own. Most causes turn out not to be cancer, and that is exactly why the rule is to check every time rather than to guess. This page explains what the appointment usually involves so it is easier to book, and it is health information rather than a substitute for being seen.
Do not wait to see whether it happens again.
What counts as bleeding after menopause
Menopause is dated backwards: it is confirmed once twelve months have passed with no period at all. Anything that appears after that point counts, however small.

That includes a spot on underwear or paper, pink or brown discharge, bleeding after sex, and a bleed that looks like a light period. Amount does not sort serious from not serious, and neither does how long ago your periods stopped.
If you have not yet reached twelve months, you are in perimenopause, where irregular bleeding is expected —
perimenopause explained
covers what is usual there, and it is a different question from this one.
Why every episode is checked
Bleeding after menopause is the main symptom that guidelines use to look for cancer of the womb lining (endometrial cancer), and it is checked because catching it early makes a real difference.
NICE's guidance on suspected cancer
treats postmenopausal bleeding as a reason for urgent referral rather than watchful waiting.
ACOG
says the same thing plainly: bleeding after menopause is never normal and should always be evaluated.

Most women who are checked do not have cancer. That is the point of checking rather than an argument against it — the only way to know which is which is an assessment, and no symptom pattern, app or online list can do it.
What can cause it
A clinician will consider several things, and this list is here so the appointment feels less unknown, not so you can work it out beforehand:
Thinning of the vaginal and womb lining after oestrogen falls, which is the most common finding.
Polyps — small growths in the womb or cervix.
Thickening of the womb lining.
Infection or inflammation.
Hormone therapy, which can cause expected bleeding patterns, and unexpected ones.
Some medicines, including blood thinners.
Cancer of the womb lining or, less often, the cervix.
Femio does not assess any of these and cannot tell you which applies. What it can do is hold the dates and details you noticed, so the person examining you has a clear account instead of a memory.
If you are on hormone therapy
Some regimens cause a regular expected bleed and some are designed to stop bleeding after the first few months. Either way,
bleeding that is unexpected for your regimen is still checked
, and starting a new one does not make a bleed something to ignore.
Tell the clinician exactly what you take, at what dose, for how long, and whether the bleeding changed when something changed.
NICE's menopause guidance
expects unscheduled bleeding on hormone therapy to be investigated rather than watched, particularly in the first months and after any change.
Menopause care options
explains what these treatments are and how they are discussed.
What the appointment usually involves
Details differ between countries and services, and it commonly includes:
Questions about the bleeding, your periods before menopause, medicines, and family history.
An examination, including of the vagina and cervix.
An ultrasound scan, often internal, to measure the thickness of the womb lining.
Sometimes a small sample of the lining taken in clinic, or a look inside the womb with a thin camera (hysteroscopy).
The sample and the camera can be uncomfortable, and you can say so. Ask what pain relief is available beforehand, and ask to stop at any point.
What to say when you book
Say:
"I have had bleeding after menopause."
That sentence moves an appointment on its own, because services are set up to prioritise it.
Add when your periods stopped, when the bleeding happened, how much, whether it has happened before, and any hormone therapy you take.
Write it down before you call. It is a short list and it is easy to lose the details in the moment. See
tracking perimenopause symptoms
for what is useful to have recorded, and
menopause explained
for the wider picture.
What not to do
Do not wait for a second episode to prove the first one mattered. One is enough.
Do not assume it is friction, or the gym, or stress, or something you ate. Those explanations may turn out to be right, and it is not possible to know that from home.
Do not stop or start hormone therapy on your own because of a bleed. Tell the person who prescribes it.
When to see a doctor
Contact your doctor promptly about
any

bleeding after twelve months without a period — one spot, brown discharge, bleeding after sex, or a full bleed. Ask for an urgent appointment and use the sentence above. Seek same-day advice for heavy bleeding, bleeding with pain or fever, or feeling faint or breathless.
Being checked and told it is something minor is a good outcome, not a wasted appointment. It is the reason the rule exists.
Seek care now:

Go to your nearest emergency department or contact local emergency services for heavy bleeding that soaks through protection, bleeding with severe pain, fainting, dizziness, breathlessness or a racing heart. For any other bleeding after menopause, book an urgent appointment rather than waiting — do not wait for it to happen again.
Frequently asked questions
Is a single spot really worth an appointment?
Yes. Amount does not separate serious causes from minor ones, and one episode is enough to be checked.
My periods stopped years ago. Does that change anything?
No. Bleeding is checked however long ago your periods stopped.
Does bleeding after menopause mean cancer?
No. Most women who are checked do not have cancer, and the assessment is what tells you rather than the symptom itself.
I bleed on my hormone therapy. Is that expected?
Some regimens involve a planned bleed. Bleeding that is unexpected for yours is still checked, so tell your prescriber.
What if the bleeding has already stopped?
Book anyway. A bleed that stopped by itself is assessed the same way.

en.title: Your Body in the First Six Weeks After Birth
en.excerpt: What changes in the first six weeks after birth: bleeding, cramps, healing wounds, breasts, bladder, mood and sleep, and the signs that need care.

children.text: Your body spends the first six weeks after birth doing a large amount of repair at once. Bleeding tapers, the womb (uterus) shrinks back, wounds knit, breasts change, and hormones move a long way in a short time. Most of this settles on its own, and some of it takes longer than six weeks, which is normal and not a sign that something went wrong. This page is health information for learning and planning, not a substitute for your own midwife, doctor or health visitor.
If a symptom is severe, sudden or frightening, skip the reading and get help. The
postpartum warning signs
guide lists what needs care today.
What the first week usually looks like

Bleeding is heaviest in the first few days and slowly becomes lighter and browner. Cramps come and go, often strongest while feeding, because feeding makes the womb tighten. Many people feel sore, swollen and very tired.
Your breasts change whether or not you are feeding a baby. Around the second to fourth day they often feel full, firm and warm as milk volume increases.
Sleep is broken. Appetite and thirst are usually large. Passing urine can sting for a few days, and the first bowel movement is often the thing people dread most.
Weeks two to six

Bleeding usually keeps fading, and the womb has often returned to around its pre-pregnancy size by six weeks. Stitches dissolve or are removed. A caesarean scar stops being painful to move around and starts being merely odd to touch.
Energy does not come back on a schedule.
WHO's 2022 postnatal guidance
treats the whole first six weeks as a period of active recovery with regular contact from a health professional, not a gap between the birth and the check-up.
Hair shedding, night sweats, sore wrists, and feet that no longer fit old shoes are all common and usually settle over months.
Bleeding, and what counts as too much
Bleeding after birth is called lochia. It changes colour from red to pink to brown to pale over days and weeks, and it can pause and restart.
Soaking a maternity pad in an hour, passing clots larger than a plum, or bleeding that suddenly becomes heavier again all need urgent advice.
CDC
lists heavy bleeding among the signs that need immediate care after birth.
Read
bleeding after birth
for what each stage usually looks like.
Your pelvic floor and bladder
Leaking urine when you cough, laugh or lift is common in the first weeks and is worth mentioning at any appointment. Common is not the same as something you have to live with.
Being unable to pass urine at all, or having no warning before you leak stool or wind, needs same-day advice. See
your pelvic floor after birth
Mood, and the difference that matters

Feeling weepy, raw and easily overwhelmed in the first two weeks is very common. Feeling flat, frightened, numb or unable to sleep even when the baby sleeps, and having it last beyond two weeks, is a different thing and is worth saying out loud.
There is no prize for coping quietly.
Your mood after birth
explains what to look for and who to tell.
If you have thoughts of harming yourself or the baby, treat it as an emergency. Femio's global
Need help now
page can help you find the next safe step.
Eating, moving and lifting
Eat and drink to appetite. There is no recovery diet to follow, and this is not a time to be counting anything.
Gentle walking is usually fine early on if it feels fine.
NICE's postnatal guidance
directs questions about returning to exercise, lifting and driving to your own care team, because the answer depends on how you gave birth and how healing is going.
What Femio can and cannot do here

Femio can hold what you notice — bleeding, pain, mood, feeding, sleep — so the pattern is in front of you and in front of your clinician at the next appointment. Femio cannot examine you, cannot confirm what is causing a symptom, and cannot tell you whether something is serious.
Bring what you have logged to
your six-week check
. A written note of a bad week is much easier to explain than a memory of it.
When to see a doctor

Contact your midwife, doctor or postnatal service for bleeding that gets heavier instead of lighter, a wound that becomes more painful, red or smelly, a fever, pain passing urine, calf pain or swelling, a headache that will not go, or low mood lasting beyond two weeks. Seek emergency care for heavy bleeding, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, seizures, or thoughts of harming yourself or the baby.
Say clearly how many weeks ago you gave birth. It changes what a clinician thinks of first.
Seek care now:

Contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department for heavy bleeding that soaks a pad in an hour, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, a seizure, severe headache with vision changes, or thoughts of harming yourself or your baby. Do not wait for a routine appointment or an online reply.
Frequently asked questions
How long does recovery after birth actually take?
The first six weeks cover the fastest changes. Pelvic floor strength, scar comfort, hair and sleep often take several months more.
Is it normal to still bleed at six weeks?
Light bleeding or brown discharge can last around this long. Bleeding that becomes heavier again, or smells offensive, needs advice.
Does a caesarean recovery follow the same timeline?
The bleeding and hormone changes are similar. Wound healing, lifting and driving are different, so follow the advice given by your own team.
When can exercise start again?
Ask your own clinician at your postnatal check. It depends on your birth, your healing and your symptoms, not on a fixed week number.

en.title: Postpartum Warning Signs That Need Urgent Care
en.excerpt: The symptoms that need urgent care in the weeks after birth, why late signs are missed, and exactly what to say when you call.

children.text: Get emergency help for heavy bleeding, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, a seizure, a severe headache with vision changes, or thoughts of harming yourself or the baby. Seek same-day advice for fever, a wound that is getting worse, calf pain or swelling, pain passing urine, or bleeding that becomes heavier again. If something feels very wrong, get help even when it is not on any list. This page exists so you can act quickly, and it is not a substitute for being seen.
Do not wait for a routine appointment, an app, or an online reply in an emergency.
Why the weeks after birth are their own risk period
Serious complications can appear days or weeks after the birth, not only during it.
CDC
built its urgent maternal warning signs list around exactly this gap, because symptoms after discharge are often explained away as tiredness.
Two things make it harder. New parents are exhausted, so feeling terrible seems expected. And attention has moved to the baby, including your own.
Say how many weeks ago you gave birth whenever you seek care, including at an emergency department or a pharmacy. It changes what a clinician considers first.
Get emergency help now for these
Contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department for:
Bleeding that soaks a maternity pad in an hour or less, or clots the size of an egg or larger.
Chest pain, trouble breathing, or a racing heart.
Fainting, a seizure, confusion, or difficulty staying awake.
A severe headache that will not ease, especially with vision changes.
Severe pain in one leg, or a leg that is swollen, red or warm.
Severe tummy pain.
Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, or feeling unable to stay safe.
Get same-day advice for these
Contact your midwife, maternity unit, doctor or postnatal service for:
Fever, shivering, or feeling generally unwell.
A wound, stitches or caesarean scar that is more painful, red, swollen, or leaking.
Bleeding that becomes heavier again, or that smells offensive.
Pain or burning when passing urine, or being unable to pass urine.
A breast that is red, hot and painful, especially with a fever.
Calf tenderness without other explanation.
New leaking of stool or wind, or no warning before you need the toilet.
Low mood, hopelessness or anxiety that is not lifting.
Some of these can be redirected to emergency care once a clinician hears the detail. Follow the advice you are given.
Infection after birth
Infection can start in the womb (uterus), a wound, the bladder or a breast. The shared signs are fever, feeling unwell, and pain that is increasing rather than settling.
WHO's postnatal guidance
treats fever after birth as a reason for assessment. Read
wound healing after birth
for what a healing wound looks like compared with one that is not.
Blood clots

Pregnancy and the weeks after it raise the chance of a clot in a leg vein or a lung. That is why leg pain, leg swelling, chest pain and breathlessness are urgent after birth even when they would not be at other times.
Do not walk it off and do not wait until morning.
High blood pressure after birth

Raised blood pressure can appear or worsen after the birth, sometimes days later. A severe headache, vision changes, upper tummy pain, sudden swelling, or feeling very unwell all need prompt assessment.
A home reading that looks fine does not cancel severe symptoms.
NICE's postnatal guidance
expects blood pressure to be reviewed after birth for anyone who had raised readings in pregnancy.
Mental health emergencies

Thoughts of harming yourself or the baby, hearing or seeing things others do not, or feeling confused, agitated or unable to sleep at all can be a mental health emergency after birth. This needs care today, not at the next appointment.
Femio's global
Need help now
page can help you find the next safe step. If you may act now, contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department, and stay with someone you trust while help is arranged.
Your mood after birth
covers the wider picture, including the difference between the common early weeks and something that needs treatment.
What to say when you call
Say that you gave birth, and when. Then say the symptom, when it started, whether it is getting worse, and anything that goes with it, such as fever, bleeding, pain or breathlessness.
Mention how you gave birth and anything that happened during it. Ask directly to be seen if you are worried and are being offered a wait.
When to see a doctor

Seek urgent care for any of the emergency signs above. Seek same-day advice for fever, a worsening wound, increasing pain, urinary symptoms, a hot painful breast, or mood that frightens you. Contact your postnatal team about anything that is not settling, even weeks later.
Being wrong about a symptom costs one appointment. Waiting on a serious one costs much more. See
the first six weeks after birth
for the ordinary version of recovery.
Seek care now:

Contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department for heavy bleeding, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, a seizure, severe headache with vision changes, severe one-sided leg pain or swelling, or thoughts of harming yourself or your baby. Femio cannot assess an emergency.
Frequently asked questions
How late after birth can a serious problem appear?
Weeks. Bleeding, infection, clots and blood-pressure problems can all begin after you are home, which is why the sign matters more than the date.
I feel awful but have no fever. Should I still call?
Yes. Feeling very unwell is itself a reason to seek advice.
Will I be wasting their time?
No. Maternity and postnatal services expect these calls, and they would rather hear about a symptom that turns out to be nothing.
What if my concern is not on this list?
Seek advice anyway. No list covers every situation, and your sense that something is wrong is information.

en.title: Healing After Stitches or a Caesarean
en.excerpt: How perineal stitches and caesarean wounds usually heal, what helps day to day, and the signs that mean a wound needs checking.

children.text: Most perineal stitches and caesarean wounds heal well over a few weeks, with the sharpest pain in the first days and a slow fade after that. Healing should trend towards less pain, not more. A wound that becomes more painful, redder, swollen, hot, or starts leaking fluid needs checking, and so does a fever. This page describes what usually happens so a change is easier to spot, and it does not replace being examined.
Perineal stitches
A tear or a cut (episiotomy) between the vagina and the anus is repaired with stitches that dissolve on their own. They usually do not need removing.
The first three to five days are the sorest. Sitting, standing up, and the first bowel movement are the moments people notice most.
What tends to help.

Keeping the area clean and dry, changing pads often, and washing hands before and after. Pouring warm water while passing urine can reduce the sting. Lying down takes pressure off, and many people find sitting on one hip more comfortable than sitting square.
Pain relief.
Ask your midwife, doctor or pharmacist what is suitable for you, including while feeding a baby. This page names no medicines and no doses on purpose.
Tell someone if pain is increasing rather than easing, if stitches feel like they have given way, or if there is a bad smell.
NICE's postnatal guidance
expects wound healing and pain to be reviewed at postnatal contacts rather than left to the six-week check.
Caesarean wounds
A caesarean is major abdominal surgery, and recovery reflects that even when everything goes smoothly.
ACOG
describes a longer recovery than after a vaginal birth, with limits on lifting and driving in the early weeks.
The dressing is usually removed within the first day or two. The scar is often numb around it, itchy as it heals, and tender to press for weeks.
Day to day.

Keep the wound clean and dry, and pat rather than rub. Loose clothing that does not sit on the scar helps. Supporting the scar with a hand or a cushion when you cough, laugh or get up genuinely reduces the pull.
Lifting and driving.
Follow your own team's advice. It depends on your surgery and your healing, and a general rule from the internet is not a substitute for it.
What healing looks like week by week
Week one.
Sore, swollen, and worse on movement. Bruising is common.
Weeks two to three.
Pain becomes intermittent rather than constant. Perineal stitches dissolve. A caesarean scar starts to feel firm and raised.
Weeks four to six.
Most people can move normally, with occasional twinges. Scar tissue keeps changing for months, and numbness around a caesarean scar can last a long time.
Healing is not a straight line, and a busy day can set it back a little. A trend of steadily increasing pain is different, and that is the one to report.
Signs a wound needs checking
Pain that is increasing rather than settling.
Redness spreading, or skin that is hot to touch.
Swelling, or a lump appearing under the scar.
Fluid, pus or blood leaking from the wound.
An offensive smell.
Fever, shivering, or feeling generally unwell.
Stitches that seem to have separated, or a wound edge that has opened.
Any of these deserves a same-day call. See
postpartum warning signs
for the wider list, including the ones that need emergency care.
Scars, sensation and time
A caesarean scar usually fades from red or dark to pale over many months. It can stay numb, tight or itchy long after it has healed, and a shelf above the scar is common.
Perineal scar tissue can feel tight and can make first sex after birth uncomfortable. That is worth raising rather than enduring — see
sex after birth
and
your pelvic floor after birth
Ongoing scar pain months later is not something you have to accept. Ask.
When to see a doctor

Contact your midwife, doctor or maternity unit for a wound that is more painful, red, swollen, hot, leaking or smelly, for a fever, or for stitches that feel as though they have given way. Seek urgent care for severe pain, a wound that has opened, or feeling very unwell.
Take a photograph if you cannot see the area yourself. It is much easier than describing it.
Seek care now:

Contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department for severe tummy or wound pain, a wound that has opened, heavy bleeding from a wound, or fever with confusion, a racing heart or feeling very unwell. Femio cannot examine a wound.
Frequently asked questions
Do stitches after birth need removing?
Usually not. The stitches used for perineal repair normally dissolve by themselves.
How long is a caesarean recovery?
Most people feel much better by six weeks, with lifting, driving and exercise guided by their own team. Scar sensation can take far longer to settle.
Is itching a bad sign?
Itching is common while a wound heals. Itching with spreading redness, heat or discharge is not, and needs checking.
Can I shower with stitches or a caesarean wound?
Showering is usually fine once you are home. Pat the area dry rather than rubbing, and ask your own team if you were given specific instructions.
The pain is worse on one side. Does that matter?
Tell someone. Increasing or one-sided pain is worth assessing rather than watching.

en.title: What Happens at a Preconception Appointment?
en.excerpt: Learn what a clinician may discuss before pregnancy, including health history, medicines, vaccines, folic acid, tests, and personal pregnancy goals.

children.text: A preconception appointment is a health visit before pregnancy. A clinician reviews your health history, medicines, vaccines, past pregnancies, and personal goals. The visit can help you make a plan that fits your needs before you start trying.
You do not need to be perfectly healthy or certain about every choice before booking.
When should you book?

You can book before trying or when you want to plan for pregnancy. An early visit may help if you have a long-term health issue. It may also help if you take regular medicine, had a past pregnancy problem, or know of a fertility concern.
ACOG
describes this visit as a review of health and medicines. Family history, past pregnancies, and daily habits may also be discussed.
If you have already started trying, it is not too late. If you are already pregnant, arrange pregnancy care rather than waiting for a preconception visit.
What health history will be discussed?
A clinician may ask about:
Long-term physical or mental health conditions.
Past surgery and hospital care.
Periods and fertility concerns.
Past pregnancies, births, or pregnancy losses.
Family health history.
Vaccines and infections.
Allergies.
Work, home, or environmental exposures.
Emotional safety and available support.
Be honest about what you know and what you do not. A missing record should not stop the conversation.
Why bring a full medicine list?
Bring prescription medicines, over-the-counter products, vitamins, herbs, and supplements. Include the name, strength, and how often you use each item if you can.

Some medicines need review before pregnancy, but stopping suddenly can also be harmful. Do not stop or change prescribed medicine on your own. Ask which medicines can continue, which may need a change, and how any change will be monitored.
Tell the clinician about medicines used only sometimes. Include pain, skin, sleep, or mood products.
What may be discussed about folic acid?
Folic acid is a B vitamin needed early in a baby's growth.
CDC
advises 400 micrograms each day for most people who could become pregnant. It advises starting at least one month before pregnancy.
Some people may need a different plan based on medicines, health history, or an earlier pregnancy. Ask a clinician which plan fits you. Follow personal advice rather than taking extra on your own.
Will vaccines or tests be reviewed?
The clinician may review vaccine records because some vaccines are best given before pregnancy. Timing matters for certain vaccines. Ask how long to wait before trying if one is recommended.
Tests are based on your history and local guidance. They may include checks for immunity, infections, anaemia, blood sugar, thyroid health, or inherited conditions. Not everyone needs every test.
Ask what each test can show and what would happen after the result. Screening estimates chance; it does not confirm that a condition is present.
What daily-life topics may come up?
A respectful visit may cover food, movement, sleep, smoking, alcohol, drug use, dental health, weight, work hazards, and emotional well-being. The goal should be support, not blame.
Tell the clinician if food, housing, money, safety, transport, or access to medicine makes planning hard. These are health issues, and support may be available.
If a partner provides sperm, their health may also matter. Mention medicines, smoking, and alcohol. Heat exposure and fertility history may matter too.
How should you prepare?
Bring:
Your medicine and supplement list.
Vaccine records, if available.
Dates and details of past pregnancies.
Key health or surgery records.
Several recent period dates.
Family-history notes.
Your main questions and pregnancy timeline.
The
trying-to-conceive guide
has useful steps. Are you worried about timing? Read
when to seek fertility help
Calendar estimates can support awareness. They cannot know the exact day of ovulation. Want to know why? Read the
fertile-window guide
These dates support conception planning and awareness. They are estimates, not a reliable way to avoid pregnancy.
What happens after the visit?

Ask for a written plan. It may include medicine changes, a vaccine or test, a referral, folic acid advice, or a date to review progress. Make sure you know whom to contact after a positive pregnancy test.
Read
pregnancy basics
for the next stage. The guide to the
first pregnancy appointment
explains what to bring once pregnancy is confirmed.
When to see a doctor

Book before pregnancy if you have a long-term health issue. Do the same if you take regular medicine or have irregular or absent periods. A past pregnancy concern also matters. After a positive test, seek prompt advice if your health or medicine needs review.
Seek care now:

If pregnancy is possible, get urgent medical help for severe one-sided pelvic or abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, fainting, severe dizziness, or heavy bleeding. Contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department.
Frequently asked questions
Must my partner attend?
No. They may join if you want, and their health information may be useful when sperm is part of conception.
Should I stop medicine before the visit?
No. Keep taking prescribed medicine unless a qualified clinician advises a change.
Does everyone need blood tests?
No. Tests should follow your health history and answer a clear question.
What if I am already pregnant?
Arrange pregnancy care and tell the clinician about all medicines and health conditions.

en.title: What Can You Expect During a Typical Pregnancy?
en.excerpt: Learn what may happen across the three trimesters, what prenatal care involves, and which pregnancy warning signs need urgent help.

children.text: Pregnancy is usually described in three trimesters, but symptoms, appointments, and tests vary by person and healthcare system. Early and regular prenatal care gives you a place to ask questions, review medicines, and check your health and the baby's development. Even a pregnancy that has been straightforward can develop urgent warning signs, so know when to seek help.
What happens during pregnancy?

Pregnancy begins when a fertilised egg implants in the lining of the womb (uterus). Over the following months, the placenta develops, the fetus grows, and the body changes to support pregnancy and birth.

Gestational age is the way clinicians date a pregnancy. It is usually counted from the first day of the last menstrual period, so the count begins before conception. This is an estimate, and an ultrasound may adjust the date.
You can use Femio's
due-date calculator
for a general estimate. A clinician or maternity team confirms which date to use for care.
What may happen in the first trimester?
The first trimester runs from the start of pregnancy through the early weeks. Common changes can include:
A missed period.
Nausea or vomiting.
Tiredness.
Breast tenderness.
Needing to urinate more often.
Food or smell changes.
Mild cramping or light spotting.
Mood changes.
Symptoms are not a measure of pregnancy health. Some people have many symptoms and others have few.
Contact a maternity service after a positive test so prenatal care can begin. The
ACOG prenatal-care guide
says the first visit may cover health and family history, medicines, vaccines, past pregnancies, support needs, and the date of the last period.
Do not stop a prescribed medicine without speaking with the prescriber. Bring all medicines, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products to the review.
What may happen in the second trimester?
The second trimester is often when the abdomen becomes more visible and fetal movement is first noticed. The timing of first movement varies, especially between first and later pregnancies.
Other changes can include:
Skin changes.
Back, hip, or pelvic discomfort.
Indigestion or constipation.
Nasal stuffiness or gum bleeding.
Leg cramps.
Changes in sleep.
An anatomy ultrasound may be offered during this part of pregnancy, depending on local care. Other tests are based on gestational age, health history, and local guidance.

Ask your maternity team how to learn your baby's usual movement pattern when movement becomes regular. There is no single number that fits every pregnancy. A clear reduction or stopping of movement needs prompt medical advice.
What may happen in the third trimester?
In the third trimester, the fetus gains size and prepares for birth. You may notice:
More pressure in the pelvis.
Shortness of breath with activity.
Needing to urinate often.
Trouble finding a comfortable sleep position.
Swelling in the feet or ankles.
Practice tightenings of the womb.
Back or pelvic discomfort.
Your care team may discuss birth preferences, feeding, support after birth, and signs of labour. Plans can change, and a change is not a personal failure.
Sudden swelling of the face or hands, severe headache, vision changes, chest pain, or trouble breathing are not symptoms to monitor in an app. Seek urgent care.
What does prenatal care involve?
Prenatal, or antenatal, care is health care during pregnancy. The
WHO antenatal-care guidance
describes care as more than tests. It includes respectful communication, health information, emotional support, and timely checks.
Visits may include:
Blood pressure checks.
Urine or blood tests.
Review of medicines and vaccines.
Discussion of food, movement, sleep, and substance use.
Ultrasound scans.
Checks of fetal growth and movement.
Screening choices.
Questions about safety, mood, and support at home.
The schedule varies by country, health needs, and whether the pregnancy needs extra monitoring. Attend the visits offered and ask what each check is for.
Screening estimates whether a condition may be more likely. It does not confirm that the condition is present. Your clinician should explain choices, limits, and possible next steps.
Food, movement, and medicines

Pregnancy nutrition does not need to be perfect. Aim for varied foods that are safe in pregnancy and fit your culture, budget, allergies, and health needs. Ask local maternity services about foods to avoid because advice can differ by country.

Movement is often safe in a straightforward pregnancy, but the right type and level depend on health, symptoms, and prior activity. Ask your clinician if you have pain, bleeding, dizziness, a heart or lung condition, or another concern.
Do not use medicine, supplements, or herbal products simply because they are labelled “natural.” A pharmacist, doctor, or midwife can check them. Femio does not provide medicine doses.
Emotional well-being during pregnancy

Pregnancy can bring joy, worry, mixed feelings, or distress. Mood and anxiety concerns can begin during pregnancy, not only after birth. Tell your care team if low mood, fear, intrusive thoughts, or sleep problems are affecting daily life.
Seek care now:
If you may harm yourself or someone else, feel unable to stay safe, or are in immediate danger, contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department. Femio's global
Need help now
page can help you find the next safe step.
When to see a doctor

Contact a clinician or maternity service after a positive pregnancy test to arrange care. Ask sooner if you have a long-term health condition, take regular medicines, had concerns in a past pregnancy, or are unsure where to access care.
Contact your maternity team the same day for symptoms that worry you, even when they are not listed below. Tell any clinician that you are pregnant and how many weeks you may be.
Seek care now:

Get immediate medical help for vaginal bleeding that is more than spotting; severe or lasting abdominal pain; a severe headache that does not ease; vision changes; chest pain; trouble breathing; fainting; fluid leaking from the vagina; fever with feeling very unwell; or a clear reduction or stopping of the baby's movement. The
CDC warning-sign list
also includes severe swelling of the face or hands and severe nausea or vomiting with inability to keep fluids down. Contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department.
This list cannot cover every urgent problem. If something feels seriously wrong, seek care rather than waiting for an app entry or the next appointment.
How Femio can support pregnancy planning
Femio's current public calculators can estimate due date and gestational age. These tools use the dates entered and cannot confirm how a pregnancy is progressing.
The fuller pregnancy-tracking experience is planned for a later release. Do not rely on an app in place of maternity care, fetal-movement advice, or urgent assessment.
Related guides explain
when to take a pregnancy test
common early pregnancy changes
, the
first pregnancy appointment
, and
pregnancy warning signs
Frequently asked questions
Is a due date exact?
No. It is an estimate used to plan care. A dating ultrasound may lead the maternity team to use a different date.
Is it concerning to have few pregnancy symptoms?
Symptoms vary and can change. Their number or strength cannot confirm how a pregnancy is progressing. Contact your maternity team about a sudden change that worries you.
When should fetal movement become regular?
Timing varies. Your maternity team can explain what to expect for your pregnancy. Once you know your baby's pattern, seek prompt advice for a clear reduction or stopping of movement.

en.title: Which Pregnancy Warning Signs Need Urgent Care?
en.excerpt: Learn which pregnancy symptoms need urgent medical care, including severe pain, bleeding, breathing trouble, headache, reduced movement, and safety concerns.

children.text: Get urgent help for severe pain, heavy bleeding, fainting, chest pain, trouble breathing, seizures, or thoughts of self-harm. A severe headache with vision changes also needs urgent care. Seek prompt advice for fever, fluid leaking, severe vomiting, major swelling, or reduced baby movement. If something feels very wrong, seek help even when it is not on a list.
Do not wait for an app, routine appointment, or online reply in an emergency.
Seek emergency help now for these signs
Contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department for:
Trouble breathing, chest pain, or a fast heartbeat with weakness or dizziness.
Fainting, a seizure, confusion, or difficulty staying awake.
Severe abdominal or pelvic pain that begins suddenly or does not ease.
Heavy vaginal bleeding.
A severe headache that will not go away, especially with vision changes.
Severe one-sided leg or arm pain, redness, warmth, or swelling.
Thoughts of harming yourself or the baby, or feeling unable to stay safe.
CDC
advises immediate care for signs that may point to a threat to life during or after pregnancy.
Which signs need same-day pregnancy advice?
Contact your pregnancy-care team, urgent clinic, or local maternity service promptly for:
Any bleeding that worries you.
Fluid leaking from the vagina.
Fever or feeling very unwell.
Repeated vomiting or inability to keep fluids down.
Pain or burning when passing urine.
New face or hand swelling.
A headache that persists or gets worse.
Vision changes.
New severe itching, especially on hands or feet.
Baby movement that is less than the usual pattern once movement is established.
Local services may direct some of these symptoms to emergency care. Follow their advice.
What can pain or bleeding mean in early pregnancy?
Pain and bleeding have many possible causes. Light spotting does not always mean a serious problem, but the cause cannot be known from an app or symptom list.
Severe one-sided pelvic pain can be urgent when pregnancy is possible. So can shoulder-tip pain, fainting, marked dizziness, or heavy bleeding. Seek help even if a home pregnancy test was negative.
Read
common early pregnancy changes
for context. Do not use that guide to decide severe symptoms are safe.
Why do headache, vision changes, or swelling matter?
A mild headache can have common causes. A severe or lasting headache, blurred vision, flashing lights, or sudden swelling may point to a pregnancy complication that needs prompt assessment.
Do not rely on a home blood-pressure reading alone. If symptoms are severe, get help even when a reading seems normal or you cannot measure it.
When does vomiting become urgent?
Nausea and vomiting can occur in pregnancy. Seek same-day advice when you cannot keep fluids down, urine becomes very dark or scarce, you feel faint or confused, or vomiting is severe.
Severe dehydration can need urgent care. Do not wait for your next routine visit.
What should you do about reduced baby movement?
Once you know your baby's usual movement pattern, a clear reduction or stop needs prompt maternity advice. There is no single normal number for everyone. Your baby's change from usual matters.
Do not wait until the next day. A cold drink is not a substitute for advice. Do not rely on a home listening device. Contact local maternity services.
What if you feel unsafe or may harm yourself?
Thoughts of self-harm or harming the baby need immediate support. They are a health emergency, not a personal failure.
Use Femio's
help-now page

to find immediate support options. If you may act now or cannot stay safe, contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department. If possible, stay with a trusted person while help is arranged.
How to communicate the concern
Say clearly that you are pregnant or may be pregnant. Explain the symptom, when it began, whether it is worsening, and any pain, bleeding, fever, or fainting.
Bring your pregnancy notes and medicine list if they are easy to reach. Do not delay leaving to collect them.
ACOG
explains why care should fit your health and pregnancy risk. After urgent care, read
pregnancy basics
. The
first pregnancy appointment guide
explains routine care.
How is this safety content checked? See Femio's
clinician review page
. Femio cannot assess an emergency.
When to see a doctor

Contact a pregnancy-care professional when a new symptom worries you. Seek same-day care for bleeding or fever. Repeat vomiting, fluid loss, reduced movement, or a lasting headache also need care. Use emergency services for severe symptoms or immediate danger.
Seek care now:

Contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department for severe pain, heavy bleeding, fainting, seizures, chest pain, trouble breathing, severe headache with vision changes, or thoughts of harming yourself or the baby. Do not wait for Femio or another online service to respond.
Frequently asked questions
Should I wait to see whether severe pain passes?
No. Sudden or severe pain needs prompt assessment.
Does a normal home reading rule out a serious problem?
No. Seek help based on severe symptoms even if one reading seems normal.
Should reduced movement wait until tomorrow?
No. Contact local maternity services promptly when movement is clearly less than usual.
What if my concern is not on the list?
Seek advice when something feels wrong. No list covers every urgent situation.

en.title: Week 10 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: By week 10 the womb is about the size of a large orange, and looser digestive muscles are behind the bloating and heartburn.

children.text: Week 10 is the week trousers stop doing up, usually before anything looks different to anyone else. The womb is around the size of a large orange now. Most women have their booking appointment somewhere around this point.
Your body this week

Progesterone relaxes the muscles of the womb so that it can expand, and it does not do that selectively. The muscles of the digestive tract loosen too, which slows everything down and is the reason for the bloating, the burping and the heartburn.

The NHS's suggestions are practical: six small meals rather than three big ones, no late-night eating, eating slowly, sipping fluids, and a short walk after a meal. Some women find coffee or rich, spicy and fatty food are the trigger.
None of that is a cure, and it does not need to be. It is a set of adjustments for a symptom that eases as the pregnancy goes on and then often returns in the third trimester for a different reason.
What you may notice

Extreme tiredness, nausea, mood swings, a metallic taste, sore breasts, indigestion and heartburn, headaches, dizziness, food likes and dislikes, a sharper sense of smell, a white milky discharge, cramping, darker patches of skin, greasier skin, thicker hair, and bloating.
The NHS adds a line worth repeating: if any symptom is worrying you, talk to a midwife or doctor. There is no list you have to match before a symptom counts.
Your baby this week
Around week 10, the figure given is about 30mm from head to bottom — apricot-sized, in the NHS's comparison. These are averages taken across many pregnancies rather than a measurement of yours.

Jerky movements are happening and can be seen on a scan, though they are far too small to feel. The face is coming into proportion, the eyes are half closed but react to light, the ears are forming, and the jaw already holds early versions of milk teeth. The NHS notes a heart rate around 180 beats per minute at this stage — roughly three times an adult's.
What care usually happens around now

The booking appointment often lands around week 10 in the UK: history, blood pressure, urine, blood tests, and a discussion of the screening choices offered later. It is a long appointment and it is worth arriving with questions written down.

Screening for Down's syndrome, Edwards' syndrome and Patau's syndrome is usually offered with the dating scan between weeks 11 and 14 in the UK. Which tests are offered, and when, differs between countries.
This week's tip

Buy or borrow one pair of trousers that fit now — not maternity clothes for later, just something comfortable this week. Women routinely spend the whole of the first trimester in waistbands that hurt because buying maternity clothes feels premature. It is not premature; it is week 10.
When to see a doctor
Contact a midwife or GP for any bleeding, severe or one-sided pain, dizziness that does not settle, or heartburn severe enough to stop you eating or sleeping.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list, and
the first appointment
explains what booking covers.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, pain in the tip of your shoulder, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Why am I bloated when I am barely eating?
Because hormones have slowed your digestion down, not because of how much you eat. Smaller, more frequent meals help more than eating less.
Is heartburn this early normal?
It is common from the first trimester onwards.
Week 11
covers the tests offered next, and
week 9
covers the peak of the sickness. Tell your midwife if it is stopping you sleeping.

seo.metaDescription: Progesterone loosens the digestive tract, which is why week 10 brings bloating and heartburn. Plus the booking appointment and what is developing.

en.title: Week 11 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 11 usually opens the dating scan window, and with it the first real screening choices of the pregnancy.

children.text: Week 11 usually opens the dating scan window, and with it the first screening choices anyone offers you. There is a lot of paperwork attached to a week in which you still do not look pregnant. It is worth reading before the appointment rather than in the waiting room.
Your body this week

Stretching muscles and ligaments can give aching pains around the stomach as things start to bulge. The NHS says to see a midwife or doctor promptly if it hurts a lot, which is a distinction worth taking seriously — ordinary stretching aches and pain that stops you doing things are not the same thing.

Blood volume is up to around 50% higher than usual, which can leave you hot, sweaty and dizzy. The placenta is close to taking over from the yolk sac, and the hormone shifts during that handover leave many women tired and emotional.
What you may notice

Aches around the bump, nausea, mood swings, a metallic taste, sore breasts, indigestion and heartburn, headaches, dizziness, new food likes and dislikes, a heightened sense of smell, a white milky discharge, cramping, darker skin patches, greasier skin, thicker hair, and bloating.
Tiredness is often the dominant one. Gentle exercise — the NHS suggests walking — helps some women more than rest does, which is counter-intuitive and worth trying once.
Your baby this week

Around week 11, the length quoted is about 41mm from head to bottom, which the NHS compares to a fig. The head is still large relative to the body, and the body is catching up quickly. These figures describe averages, not an individual pregnancy.
Fingers and toes are separating. There are tiny fingernails and small ears. Movement is happening constantly at this stage, and almost nobody feels anything for several more weeks.
What care usually happens around now

In England, the dating scan is offered between 8 and 14 weeks, and most women have it between 11 and 14 weeks so that screening can be done at the same visit. It measures the pregnancy to work out how far along it is and checks how many babies there are.

Screening for Down's syndrome, Edwards' syndrome and Patau's syndrome is offered around now. In the UK the combined test uses a nuchal translucency measurement — the fluid at the back of the baby's neck — together with a blood test. ACOG describes a similar first-trimester screening combination in the US.

The point everyone skips: a screening result is a chance, not an answer. It says how likely something is, and a further test is what gives a yes or a no. Screening is offered, never required, and what is offered varies between countries.
This week's tip

Decide, before the scan, whether you want screening — and talk it through with whoever will be with you. The appointment is not a good place to make that decision for the first time, because the scan and the blood test often happen in the same visit and the sonographer will ask. Either answer is allowed.
When to see a doctor
Report bleeding, severe or one-sided pain, or pain around the bump that is more than an ache. Dizziness that comes with a headache or vision changes needs care today.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, pain in the tip of your shoulder, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Does a dating scan change my due date?
It can. A scan measurement is usually treated as more accurate than a remembered period date, and dates are often adjusted after it.
Check where you are
before and after.
Do I have to have screening?
No. It is offered and you may decline any part of it.
Week 12
covers the scan itself, and
week 10
covers the booking appointment where it is usually first discussed.

seo.seoTitle: 11 Weeks Pregnant: The Dating Scan Window Opens
seo.metaDescription: The dating scan window opens around week 11, bringing the first screening choices. What the scan measures, and what a screening result is and is not.
seo.socialTitle: Week 11 of Pregnancy
seo.socialDescription: The dating scan window opens, and with it the first screening choices.

en.title: Week 12 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 12 closes the first trimester for most women, and it is the week the scan and the telling-people question usually arrive together.

children.text: Week 12 closes the first trimester for most women, and it usually brings the scan. For a lot of people it is also the week they start telling other people, which is a social convention rather than a medical one. Symptoms often begin to ease from around here.
Your body this week

The placenta is probably feeding the pregnancy by now, having taken over from the yolk sac, and hormone levels settle somewhat once that has happened. That is the reason sickness commonly eases in the weeks after this one.
Your waist is thickening and your breasts are larger. As the sickness fades, appetite often returns, and with it the worry about whether you are eating enough or too much.

The bump question is worth answering directly. The NHS lists what determines how big a stomach looks: hormones, pre-pregnancy weight, how many babies you have had before, and the strength of your muscles. It is a poor guide to anything, and comparing bumps with someone else at the same week tells you nothing.
What you may notice

An aching stomach, nausea, mood swings, a metallic taste, sore breasts, indigestion and heartburn, headaches, dizziness, new likes and dislikes, a sharper sense of smell, a white milky discharge, light spotting, cramping, darker patches on the face, greasier skin, thicker hair, and bloating.
Spotting still means a call, not a wait. So does any bleeding, at any stage.
Your baby this week

Around week 12, the NHS gives a measurement of 5.4cm from head to bottom — about the size of a plum. That is a population average, and a scan measuring above or below it is a matter for the sonographer rather than a verdict.

Internal organs and muscles have grown, and a heartbeat can be picked up on an ultrasound scan. The skeleton is hardening from tissue into bone. Sex organs have formed, although most scans cannot tell the sex this early.
What care usually happens around now

The dating scan usually happens between 11 and 14 weeks in England, at the same visit as screening for Down's syndrome, Edwards' syndrome and Patau's syndrome. The scan works out how far along the pregnancy is, checks how many babies there are, and looks at the physical development the scan can see at this stage.

ACOG describes ultrasound in similar terms — a picture built with sound waves, used to assess growth and dating. The timing and the exact bundle of tests differ between countries, so a UK schedule is an illustration and not a rule.
This week's tip

Ask for a printed scan photograph and ask what the measurements were. Not for the fridge — for your notes. Knowing the date the scan gave, and what it moved your due date to, saves an entire conversation at every appointment for the next six months.
When to see a doctor
Any bleeding, severe pain, a fever, or a headache with vision changes needs same-day contact.
Pregnancy basics
covers the shape of the whole pregnancy, and
pregnancy warning signs
covers what not to wait on.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, pain in the tip of your shoulder, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Is 12 weeks the safe point to tell people?

There is no medical line at 12 weeks. Many people wait until after the first scan because that is when they feel ready, and telling people earlier is equally reasonable — particularly if you would want support should anything go wrong.
My bump is much smaller than my friend's. Should I worry?
Bump size at the same week varies enormously and depends on things that have nothing to do with the pregnancy.
Week 13
starts the second trimester, and
week 11
covers the screening choices. Your midwife measures growth properly from around 24 weeks.

seo.metaDescription: Week 12 usually brings the scan and the question of who to tell. What the placenta takeover means for symptoms, and why bump size proves nothing.
seo.socialTitle: Week 12 of Pregnancy
seo.socialDescription: The scan, the telling, and the end of the first trimester.

en.title: Week 13 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 13 starts the second trimester. A small bump may appear, and sore gums become one of the more surprising new symptoms.

children.text: Week 13 begins the second trimester, and you are now roughly a third of the way through. A small bump may become visible as the womb grows upwards and outwards. For many women this is the week the constant bathroom trips stop.
Your body this week
As the womb moves up and out of the pelvis it stops pressing on the bladder, which is a relief that arrives without warning and is rarely mentioned in advance.

More blood is moving through the pelvic area. Some women find that increases their sex drive, and the NHS is clear that sex in pregnancy is safe unless a midwife or doctor has said otherwise for a specific reason.

Gums are the surprise of this trimester. Swollen, sore and bleeding gums are common in pregnancy, and the NHS advice is a soft toothbrush, gentle circular brushing, alcohol-free mouthwash, and rinsing with water rather than brushing straight after being sick — vomit is acidic and brushing spreads it across the enamel. In the UK, NHS dental care is free during pregnancy and for a year after the birth.
What you may notice

Swollen and bleeding gums, round ligament pains at the sides of the belly, headaches, nosebleeds, bloating, constipation, indigestion and heartburn, sore breasts, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swollen hands and feet, urine infections, vaginal infections, darker patches of skin, greasier skin and thicker hair.
Symptoms from the first trimester often persist for a few more weeks. Sickness does not stop on a schedule.
Burning when you pee, or needing to go urgently and often, is a reason to be seen — urine infections are more common in pregnancy and are treated rather than waited out.
Your baby this week
Around week 13, the figure quoted is about 7.4cm — peach-sized, in the NHS's comparison. It describes a population, and no individual pregnancy has to match it.

Movement is happening: at first jerky and random, later more deliberate. Most women do not feel anything until around week 17 or later. Some babies suck their thumb at this stage, which develops the sucking reflex needed for feeding after birth.
What care usually happens around now

If the dating scan and screening have not happened, this is usually the last stretch of the window — in England the scan is offered up to 14 weeks. Results from first-trimester screening often arrive around now.

The second-trimester screening test offered in the UK to women who missed the earlier window is usually available from around 14 weeks. Elsewhere the timetable and the tests differ, so ask what applies where you are booked.
This week's tip

Book a dental check-up this week. Pregnancy makes gum problems more likely, dental care is free on the NHS during pregnancy and for a year afterwards, and it is the one appointment that gets forgotten because it is not on the antenatal schedule. Say you are pregnant when you book.
When to see a doctor
Report any bleeding, severe pain, burning when you pee, a fever, or a headache with vision changes.
Pregnancy warning signs
covers the whole set, and it is worth reading once properly at the start of this trimester.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
My gums bleed when I brush. Should I stop brushing?
No — brush more gently, with a soft brush, and see a dentist. Stopping makes gum inflammation worse.
Why do I suddenly not need the toilet as often?
The womb has grown up and out of the pelvis, so it is no longer pressing on your bladder.
Week 14
continues the easier stretch, and
week 12
covers the scan behind you.

seo.metaDescription: The second trimester begins at week 13. Why gums bleed, why the bathroom trips ease off, and which infections to take seriously from now on.
seo.socialTitle: Week 13 of Pregnancy
seo.socialDescription: The second trimester begins, and the gums start complaining.

en.title: Week 14 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Appetite often returns in week 14, and the placenta is doing the work now. Some women see the first traces of colostrum.

children.text: Week 14 is often the week the fog lifts a little. Tiredness and sickness ease for many women, and appetite comes back with them. It also brings the eating-for-two question, which has a clear answer and it is no.
Your body this week

The placenta is now doing the work: pumping nutrients, oxygen and hormones across, and carrying waste away. It is firmly attached to the womb and connected to the pregnancy through the umbilical cord.
Your blood and the pregnancy's blood come into close contact inside the placenta but do not mix. That separation matters clinically, and it is the reason blood group is checked early in pregnancy.

Some women notice yellow stains inside a bra around now. That is usually colostrum, the first milk, and it can appear weeks or months before a birth. It is worth mentioning to a midwife if any breast change worries you, but its arrival is not unusual.
What you may notice

Sore or bleeding gums, round ligament pains, headaches, nosebleeds, bloating, constipation, indigestion, sore breasts, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swollen hands and feet, urine infections, vaginal infections, darker patches of skin, greasier skin and thicker hair.
Sickness, cravings and a sharp sense of smell often carry over from the first trimester for a while yet.

Sleeping position is worth knowing about now rather than later. NHS guidance is that from 28 weeks it is safest to go to sleep on your side, which is a habit that is easier to build early than to switch to in the third trimester.
Your baby this week
Around week 14, the length given is about 8.5cm from head to bottom — kiwi-sized, in the NHS's comparison. That is a population figure and not a measurement of any particular pregnancy.

The head is rounding out and coming into proportion. A midwife may be able to hear a heartbeat with a handheld monitor at this stage. Small amounts of amniotic fluid are being swallowed, passed through the kidneys, and returned as urine — a cycle that runs for the rest of the pregnancy.
What care usually happens around now

For women who missed the first-trimester screening window, the second-trimester blood screening test in the UK is offered from around 14 weeks and up to 20 weeks. It screens for Down's syndrome only, rather than the three conditions the combined test covers.
Nothing else is routinely scheduled this week in the UK. Antenatal schedules differ between countries, and a country with more frequent visits is not offering better care, only a different pattern.
This week's tip

Ignore "eating for two" and change what is within reach instead. ACOG puts the extra requirement at a few hundred calories a day from the second trimester — the size of a sandwich, not a second dinner. If appetite has come back hard, the useful move is stocking the fruit bowl before the biscuit tin, because week 14 hunger does not negotiate.
When to see a doctor
Report bleeding, severe pain, a fever, burning when you pee, or a headache with vision changes.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
How much more should I be eating?
Less than most people expect. Guidance puts it at a few hundred extra calories a day from the second trimester, and none at all in the first.
Is it too early to be leaking colostrum?
No. Some women produce it weeks or months before birth.
Week 15
covers the discharge changes that often come next, and
week 13
covers the start of this trimester.

seo.metaDescription: Energy and appetite often return around week 14. What the placenta is doing, why colostrum can appear this early, and how much extra to eat.
seo.socialTitle: Week 14 of Pregnancy
seo.socialDescription: Appetite returns, the placenta takes over, and nobody needs to eat for two.

en.title: Week 15 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Discharge increases in week 15 and hearing begins. Knowing which changes in discharge need checking is the useful part.

children.text: Week 15 brings more discharge for most women, which is ordinary and worth knowing the boundaries of. Balance starts to change too, earlier than most people expect. This is also around the week hearing begins.
Your body this week

There is more blood flowing around the pelvic area, and one effect is more of the milky fluid that keeps the vagina clean. The NHS calls it leucorrhoea, and an increase in it is expected rather than a problem.

Four changes are worth a call: if it changes colour from clear, white or creamy; if it smells strongly of anything; if it changes texture, going frothy or looking like cottage cheese; or if it comes with itching, soreness or pain when you pee. Thrush is common in pregnancy and is treated by a clinician rather than by guesswork at a pharmacy shelf.

Round ligament pain — a jabbing ache at the sides of the bump — often starts around now. Resting with your feet up helps. Itchy skin is common too, and unperfumed moisturiser, loose cotton and a cool bath are the usual advice. Itching that gets worse at night is different: the NHS says to tell a midwife or doctor about that specifically.
What you may notice

Sore gums, round ligament pains, headaches, nosebleeds, bloating, constipation, indigestion and heartburn, sore breasts, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swollen hands and feet, urine infections, vaginal infections, darker skin patches, greasier skin and thicker hair.
Being unsteady on your feet is a real and under-discussed part of this stage. On public transport, ask for a seat rather than balancing.
Your baby this week
Around week 15, the figure quoted is about 10.1cm from head to bottom, which the NHS compares to an apple. It is an average across many pregnancies rather than a measurement of one.

A soft layer of hair called lanugo is growing across the body, eyebrows and eyelashes are starting, and the eyes are becoming sensitive to light. Hearing begins around now: heartbeat, digestion, and voices from outside.
What care usually happens around now
In the UK the second-trimester screening blood test is available until 20 weeks for women who did not have first-trimester screening. Nothing else is routinely scheduled.

The anomaly scan is the next fixed point for most women, offered between 18 and 20 weeks in England. Booking systems differ between countries; if you have not been given a date by around week 17, ask.
This week's tip

Switch to cotton underwear and unperfumed soap this week. It sounds trivial and it is the single change that most reduces itching, thrush and general discomfort through the second trimester — and it is far easier to do now than after something has already started.
When to see a doctor
Contact a midwife or GP if discharge changes colour, smell or texture, if you are itchy or sore, if it burns to pee, or if itching all over is worse at night. Any bleeding is a call.
Pregnancy warning signs
covers the rest.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Can I use a thrush treatment from the pharmacy?
Ask a pharmacist or midwife first and say that you are pregnant. Some treatments are not used in pregnancy, and what looks like thrush is not always thrush.
When will I feel the baby move?
Most women notice something between 18 and 24 weeks, and later in a first pregnancy.
Week 16
covers the next appointment, and
week 14
covers the trimester's easier start.

seo.seoTitle: 15 Weeks Pregnant: Discharge, Itching and Balance
seo.metaDescription: More discharge is normal at 15 weeks, but four changes in it need checking. Plus round ligament pain, itchy skin, and the week hearing begins.
seo.socialTitle: Week 15 of Pregnancy
seo.socialDescription: More discharge is ordinary — these four changes in it are not.

en.title: Week 16 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 16 usually brings an antenatal appointment, blood test results, and the first blood pressure and urine checks of the second trimester.

children.text: Week 16 usually brings an antenatal appointment, and it is the one where results from the booking bloods come back. Blood pressure and a urine sample become routine from here to the end. Some women hear a heartbeat for the first time at this visit.
Your body this week
The bump is growing and weight is usually going on. Most of what happens this week happens in a clinic room rather than in your body.

At the appointment, the NHS describes blood pressure being checked and a urine sample tested for protein. Protein in urine alongside raised blood pressure is what clinicians look for when assessing pre-eclampsia, a condition of the second half of pregnancy that can be present before a woman feels anything at all.

That is the reason these short appointments matter more than they feel like they do. ACOG makes the same point: high blood pressure in pregnancy is frequently silent, and monitoring is how it is picked up.
What you may notice

Constipation is the complaint of this stretch. The NHS suggests high-fibre foods, regular exercise and plenty of water, and advises talking to a midwife or doctor before stopping any prescribed supplement that may be contributing.

Otherwise: sore gums, round ligament pains, headaches, nosebleeds, bloating, indigestion and heartburn, sore breasts, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swollen hands and feet, urine infections, vaginal infections, and skin and hair changes.
Some women feel the first movements from around week 17, so anything you feel now is early rather than late.
Your baby this week

Around week 16, the length given is about 11.6cm from head to bottom — avocado-sized, in the NHS's illustration. These are averages, and a scan measurement above or below them is a matter for a clinician, not a verdict.
The nervous system is developing enough for arms and legs to move. Hands can form fists. Facial expressions happen but are random, because there is no muscle control yet.
What care usually happens around now

In the UK, an antenatal appointment at around 16 weeks covers blood pressure, urine, and the results of booking blood tests — including screening for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis, and a check for anaemia. If an infection has been found, treatment and care to reduce the chance of passing it on are discussed then.
Some services also do routine carbon monoxide breath testing at appointments. Schedules and content differ between countries; ask what your own service does at each visit.
This week's tip

Ask what your booking blood results actually said, and write the numbers down. "All normal" is a summary, not a record. Knowing your blood group, your rhesus status and your haemoglobin level matters later — rhesus status in particular decides whether anti-D is offered in the third trimester.
When to see a doctor

Contact a midwife or GP for bleeding, severe pain, a fever, burning when you pee, or constipation that is not shifting. A headache with vision changes, or sudden swelling of the face and hands, needs care today.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Why do they test my urine every time?

Mainly for protein, which alongside blood pressure is one of the things clinicians watch for through the second half of pregnancy. It takes a minute and it is one of the most useful minutes of the appointment.
I have not felt anything move yet. Is that late?
No. Most women notice movements between 18 and 24 weeks, later in a first pregnancy.
Week 17
covers what early movements feel like, and
week 15
covers the week before.

seo.metaDescription: The 16-week appointment brings blood results, a blood pressure check and a urine test. What protein in urine is looked for, and easing constipation.

en.title: Week 17 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 17 is around when some women feel the first movements — bubbling or fluttering, easily mistaken for wind.

children.text: Week 17 is around when some women feel the first movements, though most feel nothing for several weeks yet. Early movements are so faint they are usually mistaken for wind. Your waist starts to go about now, which is the point most women stop being able to hide a pregnancy.
Your body this week
The womb is moving up and out of the pelvis, which makes a bump more obviously a bump. The placenta is growing too — the NHS puts its weight at around 500g by the end of pregnancy.

Stretch marks affect up to eight in ten women, according to the NHS, and they show as pink, red, purple or brown streaks depending on skin colour. They usually appear on the stomach and breasts, sometimes the bottom and thighs, and typically fade to silver after the birth.

Around one in five women feel stressed or anxious during pregnancy. Hormones can make ordinary problems feel unmanageable, and the advice is the same as in the first trimester: tell a midwife or doctor rather than waiting for it to lift.
What you may notice

Tiredness and sleep problems, sore gums, round ligament pains, headaches, nosebleeds, bloating and constipation, indigestion and heartburn, sore breasts, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swollen hands and feet, urine infections, vaginal infections, and skin and hair changes.

The NHS describes early movements as bubbling, fluttering or rolling, and notes that women often feel them more after meals, when relaxing, or when there is loud music. There is no counting to do at this stage and no pattern to establish yet.
Your baby this week
Around week 17, the figure quoted is about 12cm from head to bottom, which the NHS compares to a pomegranate. It describes a population average and not one pregnancy.
Eyes can move behind closed lids, loud noises get a reaction, and the mouth opens and closes. Fingernails are starting to grow, and fingerprints are forming — unique even in identical twins.
What care usually happens around now
Nothing is routinely scheduled in the UK this week. The anomaly scan is the next fixed point, offered between 18 and 20 weeks in England, so if you have no date yet this is the week to chase it.
If you have not decided where you would like to give birth, this is around the point services expect the conversation to start. Options differ hugely between countries and even between areas.
This week's tip

Do not start counting movements yet — instead, notice when you feel them. Early movements are irregular by nature and counting them at 17 weeks produces anxiety rather than information. What is worth building now is the habit of noticing, because from around 24 weeks a pattern of your own is exactly what matters.
When to see a doctor
Report bleeding, severe pain, a fever, or a headache with vision changes. If movements have started and then clearly change or reduce, contact your maternity service — not an app, and not a chart.
Pregnancy warning signs
covers the rest.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Was that a movement or wind?
Early on, most women genuinely cannot tell, and that is expected. It becomes unmistakable over the next few weeks.
Can I do anything about stretch marks?
Nothing is proven to stop them, and they affect most women.
Week 18
covers the anomaly scan, and
week 16
covers the appointment behind you.
