RCOG: Your baby's movements in pregnancy

seo.seoTitle: 17 Weeks Pregnant: The First Flutters
seo.metaDescription: First movements can start around week 17 and feel like bubbling or wind. What they feel like, when they usually arrive, and why stretch marks appear.
seo.socialTitle: Week 17 of Pregnancy
seo.socialDescription: The first flutters, and why they are so easily mistaken for wind.

en.title: Week 18 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: The anomaly scan window opens in week 18. It is a detailed look at development, and it does not find everything.

children.text: Week 18 opens the anomaly scan window, the most detailed scan most women have. Some feel the first movements around now, described almost universally as a gentle fluttering. A dark line may appear down the middle of the stomach, which is pigment and nothing else.
Your body this week
Clumsiness is common as the bump changes your balance. Breasts may have gone up a size, particularly in a first pregnancy.
Blood pressure is often a little lower than usual at this stage, so standing up quickly can leave you dizzy. Getting up slowly is the whole of the advice.
The line down the stomach is called the linea nigra. It is ordinary skin pigmentation and usually fades in the months after birth.
What you may notice

Stretch marks, tiredness and sleep problems, sore gums, round ligament pains, headaches, nosebleeds, bloating and constipation, indigestion and heartburn, sore breasts, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swollen hands and feet, urine infections, vaginal infections, and skin and hair changes.

Movements, if they have started, feel like bubbling or fluttering rather than kicks. Many women feel nothing for another month, particularly in a first pregnancy, and that is not a warning sign at 18 weeks.
Your baby this week

Around week 18, the length quoted is about 14.2cm from head to bottom — bell pepper-sized, in the NHS's comparison. Averages describe a population, and an individual scan measurement is a conversation with a sonographer rather than a verdict.
Hearing, feeling, swallowing and sucking reflexes are developing this week, and there is a lot of movement of arms and legs.
What care usually happens around now

The anomaly scan is offered in England between 18 and 20 weeks. It is a detailed look at physical development: the brain, heart, spinal cord, face, kidneys and abdomen, and the position of the placenta.

Two things are worth understanding before you go. It looks for a specific list of conditions and cannot pick up everything, so a scan that finds nothing is reassuring rather than a guarantee. And the sonographer is working, not commentating — long silences during the scan are normal and rarely mean anything.
The sex can sometimes be seen at this scan. Not every service tells you, and if you do not want to know you must say so before it starts. Scan timing and policy differ between countries.
This week's tip

Decide before the appointment whether you want to be told the sex, and tell the sonographer at the start rather than when they ask. It is the one thing at this scan you can control, and it is much harder to un-hear than to not ask.
When to see a doctor
Report bleeding, severe pain, a fever, or a headache with vision changes. If movements have started and then reduce or change, contact your maternity service the same day.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Does a normal anomaly scan mean everything is fine?
It means nothing was found on the list the scan looks for. It is genuinely reassuring, and it is not a guarantee, because some conditions cannot be seen on a scan.
Why was the sonographer so quiet?
Because measuring takes concentration.
Week 19
covers the same window, and
week 17
covers the first movements. If you want to be told what is being looked at as it happens, say so at the start.

sources.title: NHS: Week 18 - week-by-week guide to pregnancy

seo.seoTitle: 18 Weeks Pregnant: The Anomaly Scan Window
seo.metaDescription: The anomaly scan is offered from week 18. What it looks at, what it cannot rule out, and whether to ask about the sex before it starts.
seo.socialTitle: Week 18 of Pregnancy
seo.socialDescription: The anomaly scan window opens — what it looks at, and what it cannot rule out.

en.title: Week 19 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 19 is when loosening ligaments start to make running uncomfortable, and when sleep gets harder for many women.

children.text: Week 19 is when exercise starts to feel different. A hormone called relaxin loosens the ligaments, so the joints that used to hold you steady no longer quite do. Sleep also gets harder around here, and the fixes are all mechanical.
Your body this week

Relaxin loosens ligaments across the body in preparation for birth, and the immediate effect is that the back, knees and ankles have less support than usual. Running and other high-impact exercise often becomes uncomfortable as a result.

Staying active is still recommended. Both NHS and ACOG guidance support regular activity through pregnancy for most women, with adjustments rather than stopping — walking, swimming and low-impact classes rather than pounding pavements.

For sleep, the NHS suggests sleeping on your side, using pillows to support the bump and aching muscles, and putting a pillow between the knees. Side sleeping becomes a safety point rather than a comfort one from 28 weeks, so building the habit now is worth the effort.
What you may notice

Tiredness and sleep problems, stretch marks, sore gums, round ligament pains, headaches, nosebleeds, pelvic pain, bloating and constipation, indigestion and heartburn, sore breasts, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swollen hands and feet, urine infections, vaginal infections, and skin and hair changes.
Pelvic pain that makes walking or turning in bed difficult is worth naming at your next appointment — it is common, it has a name, and there is physiotherapy for it.
Your baby this week
Around week 19, the figure given is about 15.3cm from head to bottom — beef tomato-sized, in the NHS's comparison. It is an average across many pregnancies and not a measurement of any one.
Adult teeth are forming, lining up behind the first set that will come through in infancy. Weight is going on steadily now, which is most of what the next twenty-one weeks are about.
What care usually happens around now
The anomaly scan is offered between 18 and 20 weeks in England, so it often falls this week. In the UK the second-trimester screening blood test window closes at 20 weeks.

Nothing else is routinely scheduled. If you have not yet talked about where you would like to give birth, services generally expect that conversation somewhere in this trimester, and the options available vary between countries and areas.
This week's tip

Put a pillow between your knees tonight. It is the cheapest intervention in this entire trimester, it takes the strain off loosened hip and pelvic joints, and it is the single change most women say made side sleeping bearable rather than theoretical.
When to see a doctor
Report bleeding, severe pain, a fever, or a headache with vision changes. Pelvic pain that limits walking should be raised at your next appointment rather than endured.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Can I keep running?
Many women do for a while and many stop because it stops being comfortable. Guidance supports staying active with adjustments; ask your midwife about your own situation rather than a general rule.
Why does my pelvis hurt when I turn over in bed?
Loosened ligaments are the usual reason, and it is common enough to have dedicated physiotherapy.

is the halfway point, and
week 18
covers the scan.

en.title: Week 20 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 20 is the halfway mark. The anomaly scan often falls here, and the whooping cough vaccination is usually offered around now.

children.text: Week 20 is the halfway mark. The anomaly scan often falls here, and in the UK it is usually the week whooping cough vaccination is offered. It is also the week the measuring changes, which is worth knowing before the numbers jump.
Your body this week

Leg cramps become a feature for many women around now — sharp pains in the calf that wake you at night. The NHS advice is to rub the muscle hard or pull the toes up towards the ankle, and notes that more daytime exercise may reduce how often they happen.

In the UK, a Maternity Certificate (MAT B1) is issued from 20 weeks onwards and is what maternity pay and benefits are claimed with. Ask your midwife or doctor for it rather than waiting to be offered it.
What you may notice

Tiredness and sleep problems, stretch marks, sore gums, round ligament pains, headaches, nosebleeds, bloating and constipation, indigestion and heartburn, sore breasts, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swollen hands and feet, urine infections, vaginal infections, and skin and hair changes.
Movements have started for many women by now and are still irregular. Nothing yet is a pattern, and nothing yet is worth counting.
Your baby this week

Around week 20, the NHS gives a figure of about 25.6cm and compares it to a banana. That number looks like a sudden jump, and it is: from this week measurements are taken head to heel rather than head to bottom, because before now the legs are curled up and hard to see. Population averages, as always, rather than a measurement of any one pregnancy.

A greasy white layer called vernix now covers the skin, thought to stop it drying out in the amniotic fluid and to help with the journey through the birth canal. Activity increases week by week — kicking, turning and thumb-sucking, which develops the reflex needed for feeding.
What care usually happens around now
The anomaly scan is offered between 18 and 20 weeks in England.

The whooping cough vaccination is recommended for every pregnant woman in the UK and is usually offered around week 20, with a window from week 16 to week 32. The point of the timing is that immunity crosses the placenta and protects a baby in the weeks before their own first vaccinations at eight weeks old. CDC recommends maternal vaccination in pregnancy for the same reason, on a US schedule. Which vaccines are offered, and when, differs between countries — ask what applies where you are.
This week's tip

Ask for your MAT B1 form at your next appointment, or the equivalent where you live. Maternity pay claims have deadlines, employers need the certificate rather than your word, and it is the paperwork most often remembered at week 32 in a panic.
When to see a doctor
Report bleeding, severe pain, a fever, or a headache with vision changes. Sudden swelling of the face or hands needs care today.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Why did the length jump so much this week?
Because the measurement changed from head-to-bottom to head-to-heel. Nothing grew that fast.
Is the whooping cough vaccination safe in pregnancy?
It is recommended in pregnancy by the NHS and by other national programmes, and the timing exists so that protection reaches a baby before their own vaccinations start.

week 19

en.title: Week 21 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Balance shifts noticeably in week 21, and sleep-wake patterns are forming that rarely match your own.

children.text: Week 21 starts the second half of the pregnancy, and the most noticeable change is balance. Your centre of gravity has moved and your joints are looser, which is a combination that catches people out on stairs. Hearing is sharp enough now for voices from outside to register.
Your body this week
Feeling unsteady is expected at this stage, and it is worth adjusting for rather than pushing through. Hold handrails, slow down on wet floors, and think about a seat on public transport.

If you do fall, the NHS is clear on both halves of the answer: try not to panic, because a pregnancy at this stage is well protected — and tell your midwife as soon as possible anyway. Being checked after a fall is routine, not an over-reaction.
Sleep-wake patterns are forming, and they will rarely be yours. Naps when you can get them are the practical answer.
What you may notice

Tiredness and sleep problems, stretch marks, sore gums, round ligament pains, piles, headaches, backache, nosebleeds, indigestion and heartburn, bloating and constipation, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swollen hands and feet, urine infections, vaginal infections, and skin and hair changes.
Backache often becomes a regular feature from around now, as posture changes to carry the bump.
Your baby this week
Around week 21, the length quoted is about 26.7cm from head to heel, which the NHS compares to a carrot. These are averages across a population, not a measurement of a particular pregnancy.

The lanugo — a fine, downy layer of hair — is developing, along with hair and eyebrows. Noises and voices from outside can now be heard. The NHS notes that at this point the placenta is outweighed for the first time, which is a good measure of how much has changed since week 12.
What care usually happens around now

Nothing is routinely scheduled in the UK. If the whooping cough vaccination has not happened, this is a catch-up week: the window runs from week 16 to week 32, and it is usually offered around week 20.

If the anomaly scan raised something unexpected, this is often the week further appointments are arranged. Support organisations exist specifically for that situation, and a midwife can point you to them. Schedules and services differ between countries.
This week's tip

Take the stairs one at a time and hold the rail — every time, not only when you feel wobbly. Falls in pregnancy usually happen on ordinary stairs on an ordinary day, and the habit has to be automatic before it is useful.
When to see a doctor
Tell your midwife about any fall, even a minor one. Report bleeding, severe pain, a fever, or a headache with vision changes.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
I fell over. Do I need to be checked?
Tell your midwife or maternity unit even if you feel fine. It is a routine call and they would rather have it than not.
Can the baby hear me?
Voices from outside are audible around now, along with your heartbeat and digestion.

en.title: Week 22 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Piles and stretch marks are the week 22 complaints, while breathing practice and taste buds are developing.

children.text: Week 22 is not a milestone week, which is its own kind of relief. The complaints are piles and stretch marks, and both are common and neither is dangerous. Inside, lungs are practising and taste buds are forming.
Your body this week

Stretch marks appear as lines or streaks on the tummy, thighs or breasts. ACOG describes them as one of the most common skin changes of pregnancy, and the NHS notes they usually fade after the birth. Nothing reliably stops them.

Piles — swellings in or around the back passage — are the other frequent complaint of this stretch. They can itch, feel sore, or hurt when you poo, and the usual measures are the ones that ease constipation: fibre, fluids and not straining. A pharmacist or midwife can advise on what is used in pregnancy.

The NHS repeats a useful line this week: aches and pains are common and it is hard to know what is serious, so ask. Severe pain or any bleeding is a call to a midwife or GP straight away rather than a wait-and-see.
What you may notice

Tiredness and sleep problems, stretch marks, sore gums, round ligament pains, piles, headaches, backache, nosebleeds, indigestion and heartburn, bloating and constipation, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swollen hands and feet, urine infections, vaginal infections, and skin and hair changes.
Movements are becoming more definite for most women. Anything that feels like a change from what has become usual for you is worth a call.
Your baby this week
Around week 22, the figure given is about 27.8cm from head to heel — the NHS compares it to a sweet potato. Averages describe a population and never an individual pregnancy.

The lungs are developing and breathing movements are being practised in the womb. Small amounts of amniotic fluid are being swallowed, and what stays in the bowels becomes the dark, sticky first stool passed after birth. Taste buds are forming.
What care usually happens around now
Nothing is routinely scheduled. The whooping cough vaccination window is still open in the UK — from week 16 to week 32 — if it has not happened yet.

This is also when many services expect a conversation about wellbeing to start, rather than leaving it to the end. Antenatal timetables differ between countries; if you are unsure when your next appointment should be, ask rather than assume.
This week's tip

Do not strain on the toilet, and put a low stool under your feet. It is an unglamorous tip and it is the one that actually prevents piles getting worse, because straining is the mechanism and posture is what removes the need for it.
When to see a doctor
Contact a midwife or GP for any bleeding, severe pain, a fever, or piles that bleed or are very painful. A headache with vision changes, or sudden swelling, needs care today.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Can I use anything for piles while pregnant?
Ask a pharmacist or midwife rather than picking something off the shelf, and say that you are pregnant. Fibre, fluids and not straining come first regardless.
Will my stretch marks go away?
They usually fade to silver and become much less noticeable, though they rarely disappear.

en.title: Week 23 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Rib pain and breathlessness arrive in week 23 as the ribcage expands, and movement starts to have a rhythm you can recognise.

children.text: Week 23 is when the ribcage starts expanding to make room, which is felt as rib pain and breathlessness. Movement is becoming regular enough that a rhythm starts to show. That rhythm is about to become the single most useful thing you track.
Your body this week

Rib pain comes from the ribcage widening as the bump grows upward, and breathlessness comes from the same pressure on the lungs. Neither is dangerous by itself. Both are eased more by sitting back with your feet up than by anything else.
Breasts may start leaking colostrum, the early milk that arrives long before a birth. It is not a sign that anything is starting.
The one thing to separate out: breathlessness that comes on suddenly, or with chest pain, is not this. That needs emergency care, and the red-flag box below says so.
What you may notice

Tiredness and sleep problems, stretch marks, sore gums, round ligament pains, piles, headaches, backache, nosebleeds, indigestion and heartburn, bloating and constipation, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swollen hands and feet, urine infections, vaginal infections, and skin and hair changes.
The NHS's line this week is the one to remember for the rest of the pregnancy: get to know your baby's rhythms, and talk to a midwife if the movements slow down.
Your baby this week

Around week 23, the length given is about 28.9cm from head to heel — the NHS compares it to a large mango. It is a population average, and a scan measuring differently is a conversation with a clinician rather than a verdict.
Limbs are now in proportion. Over the coming weeks movements become strong enough to see from the outside, and the bump visibly changes shape. Breathing practice and sleep-wake cycles continue.
What care usually happens around now
Nothing is routinely scheduled in the UK this week. If the whooping cough vaccination has not happened, the window is open until week 32.

The next fixed appointment for most women in the UK is around 24 or 25 weeks, and the pattern differs depending on whether this is a first pregnancy. Antenatal schedules also differ between countries, so use your own notes rather than a general timeline.
This week's tip

Start noticing when movements usually happen — after meals, in the evening, when you lie down. Not counting, noticing. From around 24 weeks, the thing that matters is a change from your own usual pattern, and you cannot notice a change from a pattern you never learned.
When to see a doctor
Contact your maternity service straight away if movements slow down or change. Report bleeding, severe pain, a fever, or a headache with vision changes.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Contact your maternity service the same day for any reduction in your baby's usual pattern of movement. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
How many movements should I be feeling?
There is no number, and any app or leaflet that gives you one is wrong. What clinicians ask about is a change from your own usual pattern.
Why do my ribs hurt?
The ribcage widens to make room, and later in pregnancy feet also press against it.

en.title: Week 24 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 24 is the point from which a baby may survive with specialist care, and the week movement patterns start to matter clinically.

children.text: Week 24 is a threshold week. From around here a baby born early may survive with specialist neonatal care, which is why services treat this week as a line. It is also the week movement stops being a curiosity and starts being information.
Your body this week
Hunger often increases now, and the NHS is direct about it: no extra food is needed until the third trimester begins at week 28.
Weight is going on, and bump size continues to be a poor guide to anything. Some women are barely showing at 24 weeks and their pregnancies are entirely ordinary.

Aches turn up in new places — ribs, back, breasts, hips, tummy — as ligaments loosen and the pregnancy presses on things. That is the ordinary version. Pain that is severe, one-sided, or comes with bleeding or fever is not the ordinary version.
What you may notice

Tiredness and sleep problems, stretch marks, sore gums, round ligament pains, piles, headaches, backache, nosebleeds, indigestion and heartburn, bloating and constipation, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swollen hands and feet, urine infections, vaginal infections, and skin and hair changes.

Movements should now be something you can recognise. RCOG guidance is that there is no set number of movements to expect, and that what matters is a change from what has become usual for you. If that happens, contact the maternity unit — at any hour, on any day. They expect those calls and would rather have them.
Your baby this week
Around week 24, the figure given is about 30cm from head to heel, which the NHS compares to a corn on the cob. Population averages once again, and never a statement about one pregnancy.

Everything is in proportion, with growth still to come. From around this point, a baby born early may survive with the support of a neonatal unit, which can help with breathing, feeding, warmth and infection.
What care usually happens around now

In the UK, women expecting a first baby are usually offered an antenatal appointment at around 25 weeks; women who have had a baby before have a slightly different schedule. The appointment covers blood pressure, urine and the size of the bump.

From around 24 weeks, bump measurement becomes a routine part of appointments as a rough check on growth. ACOG's guidance on preterm labour is worth knowing from this week: regular tightenings, low backache, pelvic pressure, or a change in discharge before 37 weeks are all reasons to call. Schedules and thresholds differ between countries.
This week's tip

Save your maternity unit's 24-hour number in your phone this week, under a name you would find in a panic. Not the GP, not the antenatal clinic — the unit that answers at three in the morning. It is the number that reduced movement, leaking fluid and early tightenings all lead to, and looking for it while frightened is how time is lost.
When to see a doctor
Contact your maternity service the same day for any reduction or change in movement. Call for regular tightenings, leaking fluid, low backache with pressure, bleeding, or a fever.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Contact your maternity service the same day for any reduction in your baby's usual pattern of movement. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Should I be counting kicks?
No. Guidance from RCOG is explicitly against fixed counts, because the meaningful signal is a change from your own usual pattern rather than a number.
What does viability at 24 weeks actually mean?
That from around this point survival is possible with specialist neonatal care. It is a threshold in how care is provided, not a promise.

week 23
covers learning your pattern.

en.title: Week 25 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Puffy hands and feet are common in week 25, and this is the week to learn which swelling needs checking today.

children.text: Week 25 usually brings some puffiness in the face, hands and feet. Most of it is water retention and harmless. The reason it is worth a mention rather than a shrug is that a small proportion of swelling is the first visible sign of something that needs care today.
Your body this week
Swelling is common and usually caused by fluid retention. The NHS advice is still to mention it, because blood pressure needs checking alongside it.

Pre-eclampsia is a condition of the second half of pregnancy, and both the NHS and ACOG describe the signs to act on: a severe headache that does not go, vision problems such as blurring or flashing lights, pain just below the ribs, vomiting, and sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet. Those together are an emergency, and a woman can feel well shortly before them.
That is the whole reason blood pressure and urine are checked at every appointment from here on. It is picked up on a machine long before it is felt.
What you may notice

Tiredness and sleep problems, stretch marks, sore gums, round ligament pains, piles, headaches, backache, nosebleeds, indigestion and heartburn, bloating and constipation, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swollen hands and feet, urine infections, vaginal infections, and skin and hair changes.

Burping, fullness, burning in the chest and nausea after eating are common as the growing bump takes up the space the stomach used to have. Smaller meals, sitting up to eat, avoiding rich food and cutting back on caffeine all help.
Your baby this week
Around week 25, the length quoted is about 34.6cm from head to heel — the NHS compares it to a courgette. These are averages drawn across many pregnancies rather than a measurement of yours.

This is an active stage. A loud noise may get a kick, and hiccups are often felt as small rhythmic bumps. Most of the fluid around a baby by now is their own urine, which cushions and keeps the temperature steady.
What care usually happens around now
In the UK, women expecting a first baby are usually offered an antenatal appointment at around 25 weeks: blood pressure, urine, and a measurement of the bump.
The whooping cough vaccination window is open until week 32 if it has not happened. What is offered and when varies between countries — your own notes are the reliable schedule.
This week's tip

Take your rings off now rather than later. Fingers swell gradually through the third trimester, and rings that come off easily in week 25 sometimes have to be cut off in week 34. It costs nothing to do it early and it is not a decision anyone regrets.
When to see a doctor
Mention any swelling at your next appointment. Contact a service today for a severe headache, vision changes, pain below the ribs, vomiting with swelling, or sudden swelling of the face and hands.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Contact your maternity service the same day for any reduction in your baby's usual pattern of movement. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
My feet are swollen by the evening. Is that pre-eclampsia?

Swelling that builds through the day and settles overnight is very common. Swelling that comes on suddenly, especially in the face and hands and with a headache or vision changes, is the pattern to act on today.
Why does everything give me heartburn now?
There is less room for your stomach than there was.

week 24

en.title: Week 26 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Night-time leg cramps and forgetfulness define week 26, and eyes open for the first time.

children.text: Week 26 is tiring in a plain, physical way. Leg cramps at night and a general clumsiness are the two things most women name. Forgetfulness gets talked about too, and it is worth being precise about what that is and is not.
Your body this week

Carrying extra weight with a changed centre of gravity affects balance and coordination. Allowing more time for ordinary things — the walk to the bus, the stairs — is a sensible adjustment rather than giving in.
Leg cramps often get worse at night. The NHS suggests foot and ankle exercises, pulling the toes upwards, and rubbing the muscle where it hurts.

Forgetfulness is widely reported and often called baby brain. The NHS is careful about it: it is not a medical condition and is not scientifically established, and tiredness plus having a great deal on your mind explains most of it. That is not dismissive — it is the difference between a real experience and a diagnosis, and only one of those is being claimed.
What you may notice

Tiredness and sleep problems, stretch marks, sore gums, round ligament pains, piles, headaches, backache, nosebleeds, indigestion and heartburn, bloating and constipation, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swollen hands and feet, urine infections, vaginal infections, and skin and hair changes.
There is a lot of movement now. The NHS instruction for this week is unambiguous: if movements slow down or stop, contact your midwife or maternity unit straight away.
Your baby this week
Around week 26, the figure given is about 35.6cm from head to heel, which the NHS compares to a cucumber. Averages describe a population and not an individual pregnancy.

Eyes open around now for the first time, with blinking to follow. Eye colour at birth depends on genetics rather than any rule about babies being born with blue eyes, and it often continues to change through the first years.
What care usually happens around now
Nothing is routinely scheduled in the UK this week for most women. The next appointment for most is at 28 weeks, which is a larger one.
If the whooping cough vaccination has not happened, the window runs to week 32 in the UK. Antenatal patterns differ between countries and between first and later pregnancies.
This week's tip

Do ankle circles and toe pulls before you get into bed. Ten of each, both feet. It is the one thing that reduces night cramps for many women, it costs a minute, and unlike most cramp advice it can be done at the point where it matters rather than in the middle of the night on one leg.
When to see a doctor
Contact your maternity service straight away if movements slow or stop. Report bleeding, severe pain, a fever, or a headache with vision changes.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Contact your maternity service the same day for any reduction in your baby's usual pattern of movement. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Is baby brain real?
Forgetfulness in pregnancy is very commonly reported, and it is not an established medical condition. Tiredness and mental load account for a great deal of it.
What actually helps leg cramps?
Pulling the toes up towards the ankle during a cramp, rubbing the muscle, and regular foot exercises.
Week 27
closes the trimester, and
week 25
covers swelling.

en.title: Week 27 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 27 closes the second trimester. It is also the last week most airlines carry a pregnant passenger without a letter.

children.text: Week 27 is the last week of the second trimester, and two-thirds of the way through. It is also, for most airlines, the last week you can fly without a letter. If travel is in your plans, this is the week to check the rules rather than the week to be surprised by them.
Your body this week

Weight is going on and bloating and constipation are common, partly because the stomach is being squeezed and partly because of progesterone. Water, high-fibre foods and plenty of fruit and vegetables are the usual answers.
Snoring often starts or worsens, because nasal passages swell in pregnancy.

Sleeping position becomes a safety point from next week. NHS guidance is that from 28 weeks it is safest to go to sleep on your side — for night sleep, for getting back to sleep, and for daytime naps — and that waking up on your back is not a problem, you simply turn back onto your side. Building the habit this week is easier than starting it next week.
What you may notice

Tiredness and sleep problems, stretch marks, sore gums, round ligament pains, piles, headaches, backache, nosebleeds, indigestion and heartburn, bloating and constipation, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swollen hands and feet, urine infections, vaginal infections, and skin and hair changes.
Movements are strong and regular for most women. Any change from what has become usual for you is a call to the maternity unit, at any hour.
Your baby this week
Around week 27, the length given is about 36.6cm from head to heel — the NHS compares it to a head of cauliflower. Population averages, and not a description of any particular pregnancy.
The lungs are now capable of breathing, and fat is filling out folds of skin that looked wrinkled a few weeks ago. Organs continue to mature.
What care usually happens around now
Nothing is routinely scheduled, but next week is a big appointment in most systems, so this is the week to write down anything you want to ask.

On travel: the NHS notes this is usually the last week you can fly without a letter from a midwife or doctor confirming an uncomplicated pregnancy, and that cut-offs vary by airline. ACOG's travel guidance similarly puts the safest window in the second trimester and advises checking airline rules and travel insurance. Rules differ by country and by carrier — check the actual airline, not a general article.
This week's tip

If you are flying, get the letter now and check your airline's cut-off in writing. Airlines refuse boarding on their own rules, not on how you feel or how far along you say you are, and a letter obtained at 27 weeks is straightforward while one obtained at 34 weeks may be impossible.
When to see a doctor
Contact your maternity service the same day for any change in movement. Report bleeding, severe pain, a fever, or a headache with vision changes.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Contact your maternity service the same day for any reduction in your baby's usual pattern of movement. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Can I still fly?
Usually yes this week, and usually with a letter after it. Cut-offs vary by airline and are theirs to enforce, so check with the carrier before booking.
Do I really have to sleep on my side?
Guidance is to go to sleep on your side from 28 weeks.
Week 28
starts the third trimester, and
week 26
covers the week before. Waking on your back and turning over is fine.

en.title: Week 28 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 28 starts the third trimester and brings the biggest routine appointment of the second half: bloods, anti-D and glucose testing.

children.text: Week 28 starts the third trimester, and it carries the busiest routine appointment of the second half of pregnancy. Repeat blood tests, anti-D if your blood group needs it, and in many systems glucose testing all land in this window. It is also the week side sleeping stops being a comfort tip.
Your body this week
Heartburn and indigestion get worse as the stomach loses space. Backs take strain from the extra weight, and joints and ligaments are looser than usual.

Ankles, feet and face may puff, particularly in hot weather. The NHS says to have it checked rather than assume it is water retention, because pre-eclampsia can develop while you feel perfectly well and then move quickly.

From this week, guidance is to go to sleep on your side. It applies to going to sleep at night, to getting back to sleep after waking, and to daytime naps. Waking up on your back is not a failure; turn over and go back to sleep.
What you may notice

Nosebleeds and indigestion often start or worsen now. Alongside them: sleep problems, stretch marks, sore gums, round ligament pains, piles, headaches, backache, bloating and constipation, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swollen hands and feet, urine infections, vaginal infections, and skin and hair changes.
Movements should be as strong and as regular as they have been. Any reduction is a call to your maternity unit, day or night.
Your baby this week
Around week 28, the length given is about 37.6cm from head to heel, which the NHS compares to an aubergine. Averages across a population, not a measurement of your own pregnancy.

Heart rate changes across pregnancy: the NHS describes around 110 beats per minute when a heartbeat is first detectable, around 170 at weeks 9 and 10, roughly 140 by now, and around 130 at birth — all faster than an adult's, because small hearts pump less per beat.
What care usually happens around now

In the UK, the 28-week appointment includes blood pressure, urine and bump measurement, plus repeat blood tests that check for anaemia and antibodies. Women who are rhesus D negative are usually offered anti-D in the third trimester, which ACOG explains is about protecting future pregnancies as well as this one.

Screening for gestational diabetes, where it is offered, usually happens between 24 and 28 weeks. ACOG describes it as a routine screening test in that window; in the UK it is offered based on risk factors rather than to everyone. The RSV vaccination is recommended in the UK from around week 28. Which of these apply to you depends entirely on the country and the service.
This week's tip

Ask at this appointment whether you are rhesus D negative, and what that means for your care. It is the one blood result that changes what you are offered for the rest of this pregnancy and the next one, and it is the result most often assumed rather than known.
When to see a doctor
Contact your maternity service the same day for reduced movements, leaking fluid, tightenings that become regular, or bleeding. A headache with vision changes or sudden swelling needs emergency care.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Contact your maternity service the same day for any reduction in your baby's usual pattern of movement. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
What is anti-D for?
It is offered to women whose blood is rhesus D negative, to stop antibodies forming that could affect a future pregnancy. Your midwife will explain what applies to you.
Will I be tested for gestational diabetes?
It depends where you are. Some systems screen everyone between 24 and 28 weeks, others screen on risk factors.
Week 29
covers the weeks after, and
week 27
closes the second trimester.

en.title: Week 29 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Breathlessness and broken sleep define week 29, and every folk method of guessing the sex is worth ignoring.

children.text: Week 29 is breathless and short on sleep. The bump is pressing upward on the lungs and downward on the bladder, and the sleep-wake pattern inside rarely matches yours. It is also the week people start guessing the sex from the shape of your bump, which is worth taking exactly as seriously as it deserves.
Your body this week

Breathlessness comes from the pregnancy pushing against your lungs, and carrying extra weight adds to it. Leg cramps are common, and pressure on the bladder means more trips to the bathroom overnight.

Sleeping on your side with a pillow under the bump and another between the legs is what most women find helps. Resting during the day is the other half of the answer, and the NHS says plainly that if you feel unable to cope because you are too tired, that is something to tell a midwife or doctor.
Feeling excited and nervous at once is the emotional shape of this stretch. Naming it out loud to someone is more useful than resolving it.
What you may notice

Sleep problems, sore gums, round ligament pains, piles, headaches, backache, indigestion and heartburn, bloating and constipation, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swollen hands and feet, urine infections, vaginal infections, and skin and hair changes.
Balance is unreliable now. If you do fall, tell your midwife even if you feel fine.
Your baby this week
Around week 29, the length quoted is about 38.6cm from head to heel — the NHS compares it to a butternut squash. These are population averages and nothing more.

Development is largely complete in structure now; the remaining weeks are about maturing organs and gaining fat. The greasy vernix layer and the downy lanugo hair both start to disappear from around here.
What care usually happens around now

Nothing is routinely scheduled for most women in the UK this week. The whooping cough vaccination is best given before week 33 for the protection to reach a baby, and the RSV vaccination can be given from around week 28 up until labour.

The NHS also lists what cannot tell you the sex of a baby, which is worth reading before someone at work insists otherwise: the position or shape of the bump, the heart rate, home prediction kits, and a wedding ring on a string. Bump shape reflects your height, your muscles, how many babies you have had, and what you have eaten.
This week's tip

Put a pillow under the bump as well as between your knees. Most women use one and stop there, and it is the second pillow — supporting the weight of the bump so the lower back is not holding it — that changes side sleeping from tolerable to actually restful.
When to see a doctor

Contact your maternity service the same day for reduced or changed movements, leaking fluid, regular tightenings, or bleeding. Breathlessness that comes on suddenly, or with chest pain, needs emergency care.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Contact your maternity service the same day for any reduction in your baby's usual pattern of movement. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Can the shape of my bump tell me the sex?
No. Bump shape depends on your height, your muscles and how many pregnancies you have had, and none of those relate to the sex of the baby.
I am short of breath on the stairs. Is that expected?
Gradual breathlessness with effort is very common in the third trimester.
Week 30
covers the next stretch, and
week 28
covers the appointment behind you. Sudden breathlessness or chest pain is different and needs care now.

en.title: Week 30 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 30 is three-quarters of the way, and it is when vivid dreams and broken sleep are at their most reported.

children.text: Week 30 puts you three-quarters of the way through. Sleep is broken and dreams are vivid and often unsettling, which is one of the most widely shared and least discussed parts of the third trimester. It is a good week to find out what actually happens during labour, while you still have the attention span.
Your body this week

Trouble sleeping is near-universal by now, and disturbed or frightening dreams come with it. The NHS's framing is worth keeping: dreams are fuelled by hormones and by the anxiety of a large change, and talking about them puts them in proportion. They are not predictions.

If stress is persistent rather than passing, that is a conversation to have with a midwife or doctor rather than something to manage alone. Antenatal services ask about mood as a matter of routine, and there is no threshold you need to reach first.
Climbing stairs is more of an effort now, because the bump is pushing against your lungs.
What you may notice

Sleep problems, stretch marks, sore gums, round ligament pains, piles, headaches, backache, indigestion and heartburn, bloating and constipation, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swollen hands and feet, urine infections, vaginal infections, and skin and hair changes.
Movements should still be strong and regular. In the third trimester they do not slow down because there is less room — that is a myth, and a reduction is always a call.
Your baby this week
Around week 30, the figure given is about 39.9cm from head to heel — cabbage-sized, in the NHS's comparison. Averages, describing a population rather than an individual pregnancy.

Eyes can focus now, and vision continues to develop after birth. The NHS notes that a newborn can focus on a face at roughly 20 to 25cm and will not follow moving objects with their eyes until around three months old.
What care usually happens around now
Nothing is routinely scheduled this week for most women in the UK; the next appointment is usually around 31 weeks in a first pregnancy and 34 weeks otherwise.

This is the week most services suggest learning about the stages of labour, and it is worth doing while there is time. Every birth is different, including a second one after a first, so what you are learning is a map rather than an itinerary. Antenatal education is organised differently in every country.
This week's tip

Read about the three stages of labour this week, and read it with whoever will be with you. Not to make a plan — to know the vocabulary. The words you will hear on the day, from "dilated" to "third stage", are much easier to absorb now than in a room where things are happening.
When to see a doctor
Contact your maternity service the same day for reduced movements, leaking fluid, regular tightenings, or bleeding. Say so if you are not coping.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Contact your maternity service the same day for any reduction in your baby's usual pattern of movement. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Why are my dreams so strange?
Disturbed and vivid dreams are commonly reported in late pregnancy, and hormones and anxiety about a big change both play a part. They do not predict anything.
Do movements slow down near the end?
No. That is a persistent myth and it is the reason some reductions get ignored.
Week 31
covers position checks, and
week 29
covers the week before.

en.title: Week 31 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 31 often brings the first proper check of position and bump size, and the first mention of the word breech.

children.text: Week 31 is when position starts to be checked properly, and when the word breech first comes up for some women. It is early for that word to mean much. There is a final growth spurt still to come for both of you.
Your body this week

In a first pregnancy, a midwife or doctor will usually measure the size of the womb around now, from the top of the pubic bone to the top of the bump, and feel the abdomen to work out which way up the baby is.

Some babies are head down already, and some have not moved into the pelvis at all — the NHS notes that some do not engage until labour starts. Being head up at 31 weeks is not a plan for a caesarean; it is a position on one day.
If a baby stays head up as term approaches, that does change the options discussed, and there are ways to encourage a turn. That conversation belongs to weeks 36 and 37 rather than to this one.
What you may notice

Braxton Hicks contractions often start around now: the bump tightening for 20 to 30 seconds and then relaxing. The NHS describes them as painless practice contractions, and adds the line that matters — if they become painful or come at regular intervals, contact a midwife or maternity unit.

Alongside them: sleep problems, stretch marks, sore gums, round ligament pains, piles, headaches, backache, indigestion and heartburn, bloating and constipation, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swelling, and skin and hair changes.
Your baby this week
Around week 31, the length given is about 41.1cm from head to heel, which the NHS compares to a coconut. Population figures, not a measurement of any one pregnancy.

There is a lot of activity — moving, finger-sucking, the occasional somersault. Fat is filling out the skin, the volume of amniotic fluid is increasing, and voices from outside are becoming recognisable.
What care usually happens around now

In the UK, women expecting a first baby are usually offered an appointment at around 31 weeks: blood pressure, urine, bump measurement, and the results of any tests from the 28-week visit. Women who have had a baby before typically go from 28 weeks to 34.

This is also when feeding usually gets discussed. ACOG and the NHS both describe the benefits of breastfeeding, and both are clear that not everyone can or will, and that formula feeding with plenty of contact is a good start too.
Breastfeeding in the first two weeks
covers the practical side. Schedules and antenatal classes differ between countries.
This week's tip

Ask what your bump measurement was, in centimetres, and write it down. It is measured at most appointments from now on, and the useful information is not one number but the trend across several — which nobody can show you if the earlier ones were never recorded anywhere you can see.
When to see a doctor
Contact your maternity service the same day for reduced movements, leaking fluid, painful or regular tightenings, or bleeding.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Contact your maternity service the same day for any reduction in your baby's usual pattern of movement. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
The baby is breech. Does that mean a caesarean?
Not at 31 weeks. There is time to turn, some babies do not settle into position until labour, and if a baby is still breech at around 36 weeks there are options to discuss then.
How do I tell Braxton Hicks from real contractions?
Practice contractions tighten and release and should not hurt.
Week 32
covers position again, and
week 30
covers the stages of labour. Regular or painful tightenings are a call, whatever you think they are.

en.title: Week 32 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 32 is a weight-gain week for both of you, and the week the vitamin K decision is usually first explained.

children.text: Week 32 is mostly about weight — yours and the pregnancy's. Walking has probably turned into something closer to a waddle, which is your body compensating for the load at the front. This is also the week the vitamin K question is usually first explained, weeks before anyone asks it.
Your body this week
Over the coming month the NHS puts typical weight gain at around 450g a week. Fat is going on inside too, and it does a job: it helps a newborn hold their temperature, which small bodies do badly.

Most babies are head down by now, described as cephalic presentation. If yours is not, there is still time, and at around week 36 there are ways to encourage a turn that a midwife or doctor can offer.

Space is running out, and here is the point that must not be misread: less room does not mean fewer movements. NHS guidance is that movements should continue at the same rate right up until birth, and that any change in the pattern is a reason to contact a midwife or hospital straight away.
What you may notice

Tiredness is heavier now. Alongside it: Braxton Hicks tightenings, sleep problems, stretch marks, sore gums, round ligament pains, piles, headaches, backache, indigestion and heartburn, bloating and constipation, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swelling, pelvic pain, urine infections, vaginal infections, and skin and hair changes.
Pelvic pain that makes walking or turning over difficult should be raised — there is physiotherapy for it and it is not something to simply endure.
Your baby this week
Around week 32, the length quoted is about 42.4cm from head to heel — the NHS compares it to a bunch of celery. These are averages across many pregnancies, not a statement about yours.
Structurally, development is largely done. What the remaining weeks are for is weight.
What care usually happens around now
Week 32 closes the UK window for the whooping cough vaccination, which is usually offered from week 16 and is most useful before week 33.

Vitamin K is usually explained around now. The NHS describes it being offered for all babies within 24 hours of birth, given by injection or by mouth, and it is a choice that is yours to make — which is far easier to think about now than in the hour after a birth.
If a caesarean is planned, this is when practical arrangements are usually discussed, including how long a hospital stay tends to be. All of this varies by country and by service.
This week's tip

Decide about vitamin K this week, with whoever will be with you at the birth. It is offered in the first day, often while you are holding a newborn and not at your most decisive, and it is one of the few decisions of the birth that can be entirely settled in advance.
When to see a doctor
Contact your maternity service the same day for any change in movement, leaking fluid, regular or painful tightenings, or bleeding.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Contact your maternity service the same day for any reduction in your baby's usual pattern of movement. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Do movements slow down because there is less space?
No. Guidance is that movements continue at the same rate until birth, and a change in your own usual pattern is always worth a call.
My baby is not head down yet. Is that a problem at 32 weeks?
Not at this stage.
Week 33
covers packing and group B strep, and
week 31
covers position checks. If a baby is still breech at around 36 weeks, that is when options are discussed.

en.title: Week 33 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 33 is the packing week, and the week to ask about group B strep. Only about one baby in twenty arrives on the due date.

children.text: Week 33 is the packing week. Babies arrive on their own schedule — the NHS puts the number arriving on their due date at about one in twenty — so having a bag ready is not pessimism, it is arithmetic. This is also the week to ask about group B strep.
Your body this week

Braxton Hicks tightenings become more noticeable: a tightening across the bump for 20 to 30 seconds, then relaxing. They should not hurt. If they become painful or settle into a regular rhythm, contact a midwife or hospital, because that is how early labour can present.
A heavy, weighed-down feeling in the pelvis is common and often means the head has moved down into position. It does not mean labour is starting.
Tiredness at this stage is largely mechanical — you are carrying a couple of extra kilograms everywhere you go.
What you may notice

Braxton Hicks contractions, sleep problems, stretch marks, sore gums, round ligament pains, piles, headaches, backache, indigestion and heartburn, bloating and constipation, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swelling, urine infections, vaginal infections, and skin and hair changes.
Movements should not be reducing. A change in your own pattern is a call to the maternity unit at any hour.
Your baby this week
Around week 33, the length given is about 43.7cm from head to heel — the NHS compares it to a pineapple. Averages describing a population, not a measurement of an individual pregnancy.

The brain and nervous system are fully developed. Bones are hardening, except for the skull bones, which stay soft and separated until somewhere around 12 to 18 months old — the flexibility that makes the journey through the birth canal possible.
What care usually happens around now

Group B strep is worth asking about this week. ACOG describes it as a common bacterium carried by many adults without symptoms, which can occasionally make a newborn seriously unwell, and describes routine screening late in pregnancy in the US. The NHS does not screen everyone routinely and manages it based on risk factors, so this is a genuine difference between countries and one to ask your own midwife about.

The whooping cough vaccination is best given before this week in the UK for protection to reach a baby, though it can still be given later. Antenatal appointment schedules differ; the next UK appointment for most women is around week 34.
This week's tip

Store the maternity unit's number, your hospital reference number, your birth partner's number and the full address of where you are going in your phone, and write them on paper in the bag too. The NHS suggests exactly this, and the reason is unglamorous: phones run out of battery, and nobody remembers an address while having contractions.
When to see a doctor
Contact your maternity service the same day for any change in movement, leaking fluid, regular or painful tightenings, or bleeding.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Contact your maternity service the same day for any reduction in your baby's usual pattern of movement. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Will I be tested for group B strep?
It depends where you are. Some countries screen everyone late in pregnancy; others, including the UK, manage it on risk factors. Ask your midwife what applies to you.
What goes in the hospital bag?

Notes and birth plan, loose comfortable clothes, nightwear, spare underwear, nursing bras and breast pads, absorbent maternity pads, a wash bag and towels, snacks, any medicines, and clothes and nappies for the baby.

week 32
covers position.

en.title: Week 34 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 34 often brings engagement — the head dropping into the pelvis — and with it a strange sense of relief that means very little.

children.text: Week 34 usually brings an antenatal appointment, and it often brings engagement — the head moving down into the pelvis in stages. That drop can make several symptoms vanish at once, which feels like something is about to happen. It usually is not.
Your body this week

Engagement is described as a staged process, and the drop that comes with it is called lightening. Space opens up in the abdomen, which gives the lungs room, so breathlessness eases. Pressure comes off the stomach, so heartburn often improves.
That relief is not a sign that labour is close. The NHS is explicit that it can be several more weeks. What does usually get worse is the need to pee, and walking.
Colostrum leakage is common now. Breasts may feel enormous and sore, and a light bra at night and a supportive one in the day is the usual advice.
What you may notice

Braxton Hicks contractions, sleep problems, stretch marks, sore gums, round ligament pains, piles, headaches, backache, indigestion and heartburn, bloating and constipation, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swelling, urine infections, vaginal infections, and skin and hair changes.
Side sleeping remains the guidance, and the reason given is that it helps blood flow to the placenta.
Your baby this week
Around week 34, the figure given is about 45cm from head to heel, which the NHS compares to a cantaloupe melon. Population averages, and not a measurement of any particular pregnancy.
There is very little room now, with legs bent up towards the chest. Movements should still be felt clearly, and the bump visibly changes shape as they happen.
What care usually happens around now

In the UK, an antenatal appointment at around 34 weeks covers blood pressure, urine, and bump measurement, and it is where results from the 28-week bloods are discussed if that has not already happened. For women who are rhesus D negative, anti-D in the third trimester falls in this period.

The NHS also points women at the NICE antenatal care guideline around now and adds a sentence worth keeping: if you are not happy with any aspect of your care, say so. Appointment schedules differ between countries, and so does who you say it to.
This week's tip

Fix your maternity leave start date this week and tell your employer in writing. In the UK, changing it later needs at least 28 days' notice, and leave starts automatically if a baby arrives early or if you are off sick with a pregnancy-related illness in the four weeks before your due date. Knowing which of those applies is easier now than by email from a hospital bed.
When to see a doctor
Contact your maternity service the same day for any change in movement, leaking fluid, regular or painful tightenings, or bleeding.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Contact your maternity service the same day for any reduction in your baby's usual pattern of movement. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
My heartburn suddenly stopped. Does that mean labour is starting?
Usually it means the head has moved down and taken the pressure off your stomach. It can still be several weeks before labour begins.
When should I start maternity leave?
It is a personal decision, and some women work until the birth.
Week 35
covers pain relief options, and
week 33
covers packing. Ask your midwife if you want advice about stopping work.

en.title: Week 35 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 35 is the week to read about pain relief in labour, while there is still time to ask questions about it.

children.text: Week 35 is a reading week. Pain relief in labour is the thing worth understanding now, because it is a set of options rather than a single decision and you are allowed to change your mind about all of it. Sore ribs are the physical complaint of the week, and they have one important exception.
Your body this week

Colostrum may be staining a bra. It is the early milk, rich in antibodies, and some women make it weeks or months before a birth. Milk usually comes in around three to five days after the birth, and breasts get larger again then — worth knowing before buying feeding bras.

Sore ribs are common now, from a head-down position and active feet. Here is the exception: the NHS says pain that is severe, or specifically under the ribs, should be checked in case it is a sign of pre-eclampsia. Most of the time it is a foot. The point is not to be the one deciding which.
What you may notice

Braxton Hicks contractions, sleep problems, stretch marks, sore gums, round ligament pains, piles, headaches, backache, indigestion and heartburn, bloating and constipation, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swelling, urine infections, vaginal infections, and skin and hair changes.
Movements should still be as strong and as regular as they have been. Any reduction is a call.
Your baby this week
Around week 35, the length given is about 46.2cm from head to heel — the NHS compares it to a honeydew melon. Averages describing many pregnancies, not a measurement of one.
Fat is still going on, which is what will let a newborn hold their temperature. It is cramped in there, and movement should not reduce because of it.
What care usually happens around now

Pain relief options are usually discussed around now. The NHS lists self-help and relaxation, gas and air, injected pain relief, an epidural, water birth and a TENS machine, and describes what each does and does not do. You do not have to choose one, and starting with one and moving to another is normal.

Group B strep may also come up in this window: ACOG describes routine screening late in pregnancy in the US, while the UK approach is risk-based. Which applies to you depends on where you are booked, and it is worth asking rather than assuming.
This week's tip

Write down two things about pain relief: what you would like to try first, and what you do not want unless it becomes necessary. That is a more useful birth plan than a paragraph, because it survives contact with a labour that goes differently — and it tells a midwife who has never met you what matters to you in ten seconds.
When to see a doctor

Contact your maternity service the same day for any change in movement, leaking fluid, regular or painful tightenings, or bleeding. Pain under the ribs, a severe headache or vision changes need care now.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list, and
breastfeeding in the first two weeks
covers what comes after.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, pain just below the ribs, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Contact your maternity service the same day for any reduction in your baby's usual pattern of movement. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Do I have to decide on pain relief now?
No. Options can be combined and changed during labour, and a preference written now is a starting point rather than a commitment.
My ribs are really sore. Is that just the baby?
Often, yes. Severe pain, or pain just below the ribs, needs checking today because it can be a sign of pre-eclampsia.

week 34
covers engagement.

en.title: Week 36 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 36 is when position is taken seriously, and when turning a breech baby is offered. The appointment this week is not one to skip.

children.text: Week 36 brings an antenatal appointment, and it is the one people are most tempted to skip because getting anywhere is an effort. It is also the week position stops being provisional: if a baby is still head up, turning may now be offered.
Your body this week

The appointment checks blood pressure, urine and the size of the bump. The NHS makes the case for going in one sentence: these appointments pick up changes you would not be aware of, such as very high blood pressure. ACOG says the same thing about pre-eclampsia — it can be silent, and monitoring is how it is found.
Many babies are engaged by now, meaning the head has moved down into the pelvis. That still does not mean labour is close; it can be weeks away.
Leaking a little urine when you laugh or cough is common as the pelvic floor loosens. Pelvic floor exercises help, and maternity pads are worth having in the house anyway.
What you may notice

Braxton Hicks contractions, sleep problems, stretch marks, sore gums, round ligament pains, piles, headaches, backache, indigestion and heartburn, bloating and constipation, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swelling, urine infections, vaginal infections, and skin and hair changes.
Movements should not be reducing. This is the point in pregnancy where reduced movements are most often dismissed as running out of room, and that reasoning is wrong.
Your baby this week
Around week 36, the figure given is about 47.4cm from head to heel — romaine lettuce, in the NHS's comparison. It is a population average, and not a measurement of your own pregnancy.
Lungs are usually mature enough to breathe without help by now, and sucking and digesting are ready for feeding.
What care usually happens around now
If a baby is not head down, external cephalic version may be offered: a clinician applies gentle pressure to the bump to encourage a turn, and the NHS puts its success at around half the time.

This is also when the ways babies are born become a concrete conversation rather than an abstract one — vaginal birth, caesarean, and assisted birth with ventouse or forceps, each with what it involves and how recovery differs. The proportions vary between countries and so do the pathways. Ask about your own service rather than reading national figures as a forecast.
This week's tip

Go to this appointment even if you feel fine, and especially if getting there is a hassle. Blood pressure and protein in urine are the two things this visit checks that you cannot feel, and they are the two things most likely to change the plan for the last month.
When to see a doctor
Contact your maternity service the same day for any change in movement, leaking fluid, regular or painful tightenings, or bleeding.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, pain just below the ribs, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Contact your maternity service the same day for any reduction in your baby's usual pattern of movement. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
What is external cephalic version?
Gentle pressure applied to the outside of the bump by a clinician, to encourage a breech baby to turn head down. It is offered around this stage and works roughly half the time.
Does engagement mean labour is starting?
No. It can happen weeks before labour, and some babies do not engage until labour begins.
Week 37
is when full term starts, and
week 35
covers pain relief.

en.title: Week 37 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 37 is full term. A birth from here is not early, and the signs that labour has started are worth knowing by heart.

children.text: Week 37 is full term. A birth from this week onwards is not considered early, and term covers a five-week band rather than a single date. This is the week to know the signs of labour well enough not to have to look them up.
Your body this week

Around 95% of babies are head down by now, usually facing your back, which the NHS describes as the best position for labour. If a baby is still bottom-down there is still time, and some do not move into position until labour starts.

There is often more vaginal discharge, and Braxton Hicks tightenings that can feel uncomfortable without being painful. A sudden urge to clean the house is the nesting instinct, and the sensible response to it is to not overdo it.
Mood is worth a mention now rather than later. Low mood after a birth is common and it is an illness rather than a failing —
mood after birth
covers what it looks like and who to tell. Reading it before the birth is easier than reading it after.
What you may notice

As the head moves down, heartburn, indigestion and constant bathroom trips often ease. Braxton Hicks continue, along with sleep problems, backache, piles, swelling, leg cramps and the rest of the third-trimester list.

Signs that labour may be starting, per the NHS: contractions or tightenings, a show — a sticky blob of mucus that may be yellow or bloodstained, an urge to go to the toilet from pressure, back pain, and waters breaking. ACOG describes the same set and adds that early labour can be slow and stop-start.
Your baby this week
Around week 37, the length quoted is about 48.6cm from head to heel — leek-length, in the NHS's comparison. Population averages, and not a measurement of your own pregnancy.

Facial expressions are being tried out, and they are random rather than emotional. By now most women know when their baby is usually active and when they are calmer, which is exactly the knowledge that matters if anything changes.
What care usually happens around now
Group B strep may be discussed if it has not been already. In some countries screening happens routinely late in pregnancy; in the UK it is managed on risk factors.

If you are expecting twins, the NHS notes that most twin pregnancies do not go beyond 38 weeks, so the timeline is different and specialist. Antenatal schedules for the last month differ between countries, and this is the point where knowing your own service's plan matters more than any general guide.
This week's tip

Call your maternity unit for anything you are unsure about, and do it without rehearsing first. From full term onwards the cost of a call that turns out to be nothing is a few minutes, and units expect them. The thing that gets people into trouble at 37 weeks is deciding in advance that a symptom is probably fine.
When to see a doctor
Contact your maternity service the same day for any change in movement, leaking fluid, regular or painful tightenings, or bleeding.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, pain just below the ribs, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Contact your maternity service the same day for any reduction in your baby's usual pattern of movement. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Is 37 weeks too early?
No. From 37 weeks a birth is described as full term, and term runs across a five-week band up to 42 weeks.
What is a show?
A sticky blob of mucus, sometimes yellow or bloodstained, that plugged the cervix. It can be one of the first signs labour is coming, and it can still be days away.
Week 38
covers the next appointment, and
week 36
covers position.
