en.title: Week 38 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 38 is when the conversation about going past 41 weeks usually happens, and when waiting becomes the main symptom.

children.text: Week 38 is full term and mostly waiting. The appointment around now usually includes a conversation about what happens if the pregnancy goes past 41 weeks, which is a conversation worth having while nothing is urgent. Frustration and boredom are, genuinely, this week's new symptoms.
Your body this week
At the appointment, a midwife or doctor measures the bump with a tape, checks blood pressure, and looks for protein in urine — the pre-eclampsia checks that continue right to the end.
If a caesarean is planned, the NHS notes it is usually booked from at least 39 weeks, to give the lungs the best chance of being fully developed.

The induction conversation happens now rather than later. Both the NHS and ACOG describe induction as bringing labour on artificially, and both describe it as something offered and discussed rather than imposed. The NHS puts the proportion of labours started this way at around one in five.
What you may notice

Braxton Hicks contractions, sleep problems, stretch marks, sore gums, round ligament pains, piles, headaches, backache, indigestion and heartburn, bloating and constipation, leg cramps, feeling hot, dizziness, swelling, urine infections, vaginal infections, and skin and hair changes.
Everybody will now be texting to ask whether anything has happened. That is its own kind of symptom and the answer to it is a group message sent once.
Your baby this week
Around week 38, the figure given is about 49.8cm from head to heel, which the NHS compares to a stick of rhubarb. Averages across many pregnancies, not a measurement of one.
The downy lanugo hair is mostly gone, though some babies are born with patches. Meconium — the dark, sticky first stool — is collecting in the bowels and normally passes after the birth.
What care usually happens around now
In the UK an antenatal appointment around 38 weeks covers blood pressure, urine and bump measurement, and includes the discussion about going past 41 weeks.

What is offered then differs between countries and services: NHS guidance describes induction being offered if labour has not started by 41 weeks, with increased monitoring offered to women who decline, and a further offer if a pregnancy reaches 42 weeks. ACOG describes induction decisions made with a clinician on the basis of the individual pregnancy. Neither treats the due date itself as a deadline.
This week's tip

Ask now what your service does at 41 and 42 weeks, and what happens if you would rather wait. Both are real options with real trade-offs, and the version of this conversation that happens calmly at 38 weeks is a much better one than the version that happens in a clinic corridor when you are exhausted and overdue.
When to see a doctor
Contact your maternity service the same day for any change in movement, leaking fluid, regular or painful tightenings, or bleeding.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, pain just below the ribs, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Contact your maternity service the same day for any reduction in your baby's usual pattern of movement. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Can I say no to induction?
Yes. It is offered, and declining is a decision your service should support with a plan for extra monitoring. Ask what that plan is.
Why is a planned caesarean not booked before 39 weeks?
Because the last weeks matter for lung development, so planned caesareans are usually scheduled from 39 weeks.
Week 39
covers waters breaking, and
week 37
covers the start of full term.

en.title: Week 39 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 39 is when waters may break, and when knowing exactly when to call the maternity unit matters more than anything else.

children.text: Week 39 is when most women go into labour within a week either side of their due date. Waters can break at any time, and almost never the way films show it. What is worth knowing precisely this week is when to pick up the phone.
Your body this week

More discharge is usual, and it should be thin, white and without much smell. A show — a slimy blob of mucus, sometimes yellow or bloodstained — is the plug that sealed the cervix coming away. It can mean labour is coming and it can still be days off.
Back pain often increases as the head presses against the spine, and there is more pressure at the bottom of the bump. Sudden bursts of energy and an urge to tidy are the nesting instinct.

On waters breaking, the NHS is specific: do not expect a tidal wave — it may be a trickle. If you think it has happened, call your midwife or maternity unit for advice, because once waters have broken there is a greater risk of infection and your care may change.
What you may notice

Practice contractions can be frequent now. The NHS's threshold for calling is clear: phone the hospital or midwife when contractions last at least 60 seconds and come every five minutes — or at any time if something worries you, such as movements stopping or any bleeding.
Also expect: sleep problems, backache, piles, indigestion and heartburn, leg cramps, swelling, dizziness, and everything else the third trimester has been offering for weeks.
Your baby this week
Around week 39, the length quoted is about 50.7cm from head to heel — the NHS compares it to a small watermelon. These are averages describing many pregnancies, not a measurement of one.
The skin has grown a tougher outer layer that protects and helps with temperature. The waxy vernix coating may still be there at birth or may be mostly gone, and both are ordinary.
What care usually happens around now
Nothing is routinely scheduled for most women this week, and appointments resume at 40 and 41 weeks in the UK for a first baby.

Two lists are worth reading before the birth rather than after. The NHS names nine signs that should be treated as an emergency at this stage: any bleeding, brown or pink discharge, severe itching particularly at night, a headache that will not go, vision problems, pain just below the ribs, extreme swelling of the feet, ankles, hands and face, persistent stomach pains, and a temperature above 37.5C with no cold or flu symptoms. The second list is what a newborn is actually like in the first minutes — often quiet before crying, blue hands and feet, irregular breathing — because knowing that in advance prevents a great deal of fright.
This week's tip

Agree with your birth partner tonight who calls the unit and who drives. It sounds absurdly small. It is the thing that reliably falls apart at 3am, and the version where both of you already know the answer is the version that works.
When to see a doctor
Call your maternity unit when contractions last 60 seconds and come every five minutes, or at any time if waters break, movements change, or you have bleeding.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, pain just below the ribs, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Contact your maternity service the same day for any reduction in your baby's usual pattern of movement. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
How do I know if my waters have broken?
You often cannot be certain, which is why the advice is to call and be assessed rather than to work it out at home. It may be a trickle rather than a gush.
When exactly should I go in?
The usual guidance is contractions lasting 60 seconds coming every five minutes, and any time you are worried.
Week 40
covers the due date and beyond, and
week 38
covers the induction conversation.

en.title: Week 4 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 4 is usually the week a period is missed. Nothing shows on the outside, and many women feel no different at all.

children.text: Week 4 is usually the week a period is missed, which is how most pregnancies are first noticed. Nothing shows on the outside yet, and plenty of women feel no different at all. Pregnancy is dated from the first day of the last period, so week 4 falls roughly two weeks after conception rather than four.
Your body this week

Almost nothing is visible. The NHS notes that in a first pregnancy many women do not start to show until at least week 12, and that women who have been pregnant before sometimes show sooner because the muscles of the womb and belly have stretched already.
Inside, the pregnancy hormone human chorionic gonadotrophin is rising. It is the hormone home pregnancy tests look for, which is why a test can turn positive before there is anything to feel or see.

The dating question confuses almost everyone at this point. Counting from the last period is a convention, not a claim about when conception happened, and it is the reason a "4 weeks pregnant" result can arrive only days after a missed period.
Work out where you are
if the numbers do not seem to line up.
What you may notice

Possibly nothing. The NHS lists a missed period as often the first sign, alongside sore breasts, a metallic taste, tiredness, nausea at any time of day, a heightened sense of smell, needing to pee more often, new food likes and dislikes, and a milky white vaginal discharge.

Some women notice light spotting around now. Light spotting is common in early pregnancy, but the NHS advice is to tell a doctor or midwife about any bleeding in pregnancy rather than deciding for yourself what it is.
Cramping a little like period pain is also common. Severe pain, particularly on one side, is not something to wait out — see the red-flag box below.
If none of this is happening to you, that is not a warning sign. Symptoms in early pregnancy vary enormously from woman to woman and from pregnancy to pregnancy.
Your baby this week

Around week 4, an embryo is about 2mm long — roughly the size of a poppy seed, in the NHS's own illustration. Those figures describe averages across many pregnancies, not a measurement of any particular one.

At this stage the embryo sits inside an amniotic sac filled with cushioning fluid, attached to a small yolk sac that supplies everything it needs for now. The outer layer of cells will go on to become the placenta.
What care usually happens around now

Nothing is scheduled this week in most systems, but this is when many women make first contact. NHS guidance is to see a GP or refer yourself to a midwife as soon as you know, because the first full appointment — the booking appointment — usually happens between weeks 8 and 12 and takes about an hour.

Guidelines also recommend a folic acid supplement in early pregnancy, which is why the first conversation matters more than the first scan. Antenatal schedules differ between countries, so what is offered near you may not match a UK timeline.
This week's tip

Write down the first day of your last period, and keep it somewhere you will not lose it. Every date offered to you for the next nine months is calculated from it, and it is the single question you will be asked at every first appointment. If your cycles are irregular and you genuinely do not know, say so — a dating scan exists for exactly that reason.
When to see a doctor
Contact a midwife, GP or maternity service if you have any bleeding, if pain is severe or one-sided, or if you feel faint.
Pregnancy warning signs
covers the full list. If a positive test has not been confirmed yet,
when to take a pregnancy test
explains the timing.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, pain in the tip of your shoulder, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Why am I 4 weeks pregnant if I only just conceived?
Because the count starts at the first day of your last period, about two weeks before conception. It is a shared convention so that everyone measures the same way.
I have no symptoms at all. Is that a problem?
No. Many women have no symptoms in week 4, and the absence of symptoms says nothing about how a pregnancy is going.
Week 5
is when a lot of women first notice something.

en.title: Week 40 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 40 contains the due date, which is an estimate rather than a deadline. Term runs to 42 weeks, and nothing is late inside it.

children.text: Week 40 contains the due date, and the due date is an estimate rather than a deadline. Term runs from 37 to 42 weeks, which means a birth anywhere in that five-week band is on time. Nothing about week 41 makes a pregnancy late.
Your body this week

In a first pregnancy there is usually an antenatal appointment this week: blood pressure, bump measurement, and a urine sample checked for protein. The pre-eclampsia checks continue right to the end because the condition can appear right to the end.
Practice contractions are frequent and should not hurt. Real contractions do: the bump goes tight and painful, then the pain goes as the muscles relax.

The NHS describes labour in three stages — contractions opening the cervix to about 10cm, the birth itself, and the placenta being delivered — and puts the first stage at roughly 6 to 12 hours, often less for women who have given birth before.
What you may notice
Something like premenstrual heaviness, or a low backache, can be an early sign. Alongside: practice contractions, sleep problems, backache, piles, indigestion, leg cramps, swelling and dizziness.

The call threshold is unchanged: contact the unit when contractions last at least 60 seconds and come every five minutes, and at any time if waters break, if there is bleeding, or if movements change.

Movements matter as much this week as any other. The NHS says plainly that movements should not slow down or stop, and that a change is a reason to contact the maternity unit straight away, at any hour.
Your baby this week
Around week 40, the length given is about 51.2cm from head to heel — pumpkin-sized, in the NHS's comparison. It is a population average and never a measurement of an individual pregnancy.
It is cramped, and movements continue in their usual pattern regardless.
What care usually happens around now

If labour has not started, the conversation moves to what happens next. NHS guidance is that induction is offered if labour has not begun by 41 weeks, and that women who prefer to wait should be offered increased monitoring of their own and their baby's wellbeing, with a further offer if a pregnancy reaches 42 weeks. ACOG describes the same decision being made with a clinician, weighing the individual pregnancy.

There are no proven ways to safely bring on labour at home, and the NHS advises checking with a midwife or doctor before trying anything beyond waiting. What is offered, and when, differs between countries.
This week's tip

Stop counting days past the due date and start counting weeks of term. The due date was calculated from a period date or a scan and it was always an estimate. Reframing the wait as "somewhere in a five-week window" is not a consolation — it is a more accurate description of what a due date is, and it is what makes the last fortnight bearable.
When to see a doctor
Call the maternity unit for contractions lasting 60 seconds every five minutes, for waters breaking, for bleeding, or for any change in movement.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list, and
postpartum recovery in the first six weeks
covers what comes next.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, pain just below the ribs, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Contact your maternity service the same day for any reduction in your baby's usual pattern of movement. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Is my baby late?
No. Term is 37 to 42 weeks, and a due date is a single estimated point inside a five-week band. Most women give birth in the week either side of it.
Can I do anything to bring on labour?
There are no proven safe home methods, and the advice is to ask a midwife or doctor before trying anything.
Week 39
covers waters and shows, and your service will discuss what happens at 41 and 42 weeks.

en.title: Week 5 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 5 is when most women find out. Tiredness often arrives first, and the heart and nervous system are taking shape.

children.text: Week 5 is when a great many women find out. A missed period has usually registered by now, and home tests are reliable at this point. Excitement and worry arriving together is ordinary, not a sign that anything is wrong.
Your body this week
There is still nothing to see. What there is, is tiredness — the kind the NHS describes as extreme, and the kind that is hard to explain to anyone who does not know yet.

Hormone levels are climbing steeply, and they are behind most of what you feel. Some women notice light bleeding around this time and assume it is a period arriving late. It can also be implantation bleeding, when the embryo attaches to the lining of the womb.

Worry is common enough to be worth naming. NHS guidance points out that around one in five women feel anxious or stressed during pregnancy, and it advises talking to a midwife or doctor rather than sitting with it. That is not a sign of coping badly. It is the most-reported feeling of the first trimester after tiredness.
What you may notice

The NHS lists tiredness, a metallic taste, sore breasts, nausea at any hour, mood swings, new food likes and dislikes, a sharper sense of smell, needing to pee more often, a milky white discharge, cramping like period pain, and light spotting.
Food cravings and aversions can start now. Both come from hormones changing how taste and smell work, and neither predicts anything about the pregnancy.
Two things do not belong on a wait-and-see list: heavy bleeding, and pain that is severe or concentrated on one side. Both need to be assessed today.
Your baby this week
Around week 5, an embryo is roughly 2mm long — about the size of a sesame seed, as the NHS illustrates it. These are population figures, and no woman's own pregnancy has to match them.

This is the week the heart begins to form and beat, and the brain and spinal cord are taking shape rapidly. Blood vessels are appearing, and some of them will become the umbilical cord. The placenta is being built and will eventually take over from the yolk sac.
What care usually happens around now

Nothing is routinely scheduled. This is the week to make contact if you have not: the first booking appointment usually falls between weeks 8 and 12 in the UK, and services elsewhere run to different timetables.

If you take medication for an existing condition, guidance is to tell your prescriber that you are pregnant rather than stopping anything on your own. That single conversation is more useful this month than any other.
This week's tip

Book the midwife or GP appointment today rather than after the weekend. Waiting lists exist, the booking appointment takes about an hour, and every screening choice offered later has a window attached to it. Getting into the system early is the one thing this week that changes what is available to you in weeks 11 to 14.
When to see a doctor
Any bleeding should be reported, even if it settles. So should severe pain, one-sided pain, pain at the tip of the shoulder, or feeling faint.
Early pregnancy changes
covers what is ordinary this early, and
pregnancy warning signs
covers what is not.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, pain in the tip of your shoulder, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
I bled a little and I am still testing positive. What does that mean?

It needs to be assessed rather than interpreted at home. Light spotting is common and often harmless, and it can also be the first sign of something that needs care today. Contact a midwife, GP or early pregnancy unit.
Should the tiredness be this bad?
For many women it is, and it usually eases in the second trimester.
Week 6
covers the nausea that often arrives next, and
week 4
explains why the counting starts where it does. If tiredness is stopping you functioning, say so at your first appointment.

en.title: Week 6 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 6 is when nausea often starts, at any hour of the day. Limb buds and ears are beginning to form.

children.text: Week 6 is when nausea most often turns up, and it rarely keeps to mornings. The name is one of the least accurate in medicine. Meanwhile arms, legs and ears are starting to form, all inside something the size of a pea.
Your body this week
Outwardly, nothing. Inwardly, hormones are running at a level most women feel. Nausea, exhaustion and a sense of smell that has become a liability are the three complaints of this week.

The NHS describes morning sickness as something that can happen at any time of day, though it is often worse on waking. Its practical suggestions are unglamorous and do help some women: a snack by the bed, six small meals rather than three large ones, plenty of fluids, and rest. Some find ginger useful, or ice cubes, or acupressure wristbands.

What matters more than any of those is the line where it stops being ordinary. If you cannot keep food or fluids down, that is a reason to contact a midwife or doctor rather than to endure it. ACOG describes severe, persistent nausea and vomiting in pregnancy as a condition clinicians assess and manage, not a rite of passage.
What you may notice

Alongside nausea and tiredness: a metallic taste, sore breasts, mood swings, headaches, new food likes and dislikes, a sharper sense of smell, needing to pee more often, a white milky discharge, cramping like period pain, and bloating.
Many women feel considerably better after the first trimester ends at week 12, which is a long way off when you are in the middle of week 6.
Bleeding, severe pain and one-sided pain are the three things not to wait on. Contact a service today.
Your baby this week

Around week 6, an embryo measures roughly 6mm — the NHS compares it to a pea, and notes some people think it looks like a tadpole with a small tail. The figures are averages drawn from many pregnancies rather than a description of anyone's own.

Arms and legs are appearing as limb buds. There are dents where the ears will be, a bump where the heart is, and another where the head will be. A heartbeat can sometimes be seen on a vaginal ultrasound scan at this stage, though in most systems no scan is offered this early unless there is a specific reason.
What care usually happens around now

Still nothing routine for most women. If you have had fertility treatment, an early scan may be part of your care, and if you have had an ectopic pregnancy before, guidance is usually to be seen early. Both are individual reasons rather than a general schedule, and schedules differ between countries.
This week's tip

Eat something before you get out of bed — literally before your feet touch the floor. Nausea is often worst on an empty stomach after a night's gap, and putting a packet of plain biscuits or crackers on the bedside table the night before is the version of this advice that actually works, because it does not require you to feel well enough to go to the kitchen.
When to see a doctor
Contact a midwife or GP if you cannot keep fluids down, if you are losing weight, if you feel dizzy on standing, or if you are passing very little urine. Any bleeding should be reported.
Pregnancy warning signs
has the full list.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, pain in the tip of your shoulder, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
My nausea stopped suddenly. Should I worry?
Symptoms come and go, and many women have a good day in the middle of a bad fortnight. It is not something to interpret alone either way — if it worries you, ring your midwife and say so.
Is it normal to feel sick all day?
Yes, and the name misleads people.
Week 7
and
week 5
cover the same stretch. If you cannot keep anything down, that is the point at which to ask for help.

en.title: Week 7 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Blood volume is already climbing in week 7, which explains the thirst and the dizziness. Brain and spinal cord are growing fast.

children.text: By week 7 there is noticeably more blood moving around your body than there was seven weeks ago. That is behind a lot of the thirst, the warmth and the head-rush on standing. Nothing is visible yet, and most women are still deciding who to tell.
Your body this week

Blood volume rises through pregnancy, and the NHS puts the eventual increase at up to 50%. The extra blood supplies the womb with the oxygen and nutrients a pregnancy needs, and the immediate effect on you is thirst.

The NHS suggests aiming for around eight medium glasses of fluid a day — water, milk, fruit juice or fruit tea all count. Feeling hot, sweaty or lightheaded is common at this stage and usually settles with sitting down.

The womb is around the size of a lemon this week. In a first pregnancy most women do not look pregnant until about week 12; those who have been pregnant before often show earlier because the muscles have stretched before.
What you may notice

Sickness, tiredness and mood swings are the trio most women name. Add a metallic taste, sore breasts, headaches, a heightened sense of smell, a white milky discharge, cramping, bloating, and skin changes such as darker patches on the face.

One symptom deserves separating out even though it sounds minor. Itching all over, particularly if it is worse at night, is something the NHS says to report rather than treat with moisturiser and hope. Tell a midwife or doctor.

Anything that feels strange to you is worth raising, even if it is not on a list. Most of it turns out to be ordinary, and the point of asking is that neither you nor an app is the right thing to be deciding with.
Your baby this week

Around week 7, an embryo measures about 10mm from head to bottom — roughly grape-sized, as the NHS puts it. Averages are all these numbers are, and a scan measuring differently is not a verdict on anything.

The brain grows faster than the rest of the body at this stage, so the forehead is large. There are dimples where the nose and ears will be, eyelids are beginning to form, and the limb buds are laying down cartilage that will become bones.
What care usually happens around now
Most women are waiting for the booking appointment, which usually falls between weeks 8 and 12 in the UK and takes about an hour.
What happens at the first pregnancy appointment
covers what is asked and offered.

Legally, in the UK, an employer does not have to be told until the 15th week before the baby is due. Telling them earlier unlocks paid time off for antenatal appointments and a workplace risk assessment. Employment rules are national, so check what applies where you live.
This week's tip

Fill a bottle in the morning and finish it by evening. Thirst in early pregnancy is real and mostly unnoticed until you are dizzy, and the difference between "I should drink more" and a container you can see the level in is the difference between intending and doing.
When to see a doctor
Report any bleeding, severe or one-sided pain, itching all over, or dizziness that does not settle when you sit.
Pregnancy warning signs
lists the rest.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, pain in the tip of your shoulder, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
Do I have to tell my employer yet?
Not usually this early. In the UK the deadline is the 15th week before the baby is due, and telling them sooner brings maternity rights forward, including paid antenatal appointments.
Why am I dizzy when I stand up?
Blood volume and blood pressure both change in pregnancy.
Week 8
covers more of the same stretch, and
week 6
covers the sickness. Dizziness that comes with a headache, vision changes or fainting needs care today.

en.title: Week 8 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 8 usually opens the booking appointment window, and it is often the week mood swings become the loudest symptom.

children.text: Week 8 usually opens the window for the booking appointment, the longest antenatal appointment most women have. It is also, for many, the week mood becomes the loudest symptom rather than sickness. Both are worth planning for.
Your body this week
You may be bloated and your breasts slightly swollen, but it will probably be several more weeks before you look pregnant.

The placenta is preparing to take over the work of feeding the pregnancy and removing waste. The NHS describes it as sprouting small branches that anchor it to the wall of the womb. That handover is gradual and finishes early in the second trimester.

Feeling anxious or low is common enough that NHS antenatal care asks about it directly. The advice is to say so — to a midwife, to a GP, to someone — rather than to wait and see whether it lifts. There is no threshold you have to reach before it is worth mentioning.
What you may notice
Tiredness, sickness and needing to pee more often as the growing womb presses on the bladder. If that is wrecking your sleep, the NHS suggests drinking plenty during the day and less in the evening.

The rest of the list is familiar by now: a metallic taste, sore breasts, headaches, mood swings, food likes and dislikes, a sharper sense of smell, a milky white discharge, cramping, darker patches of skin, and bloating.
Bleeding, severe pain or one-sided pain still belong to today rather than to the next appointment.
Your baby this week

Around week 8, the measurement given is roughly 16mm from head to bottom — about raspberry-sized in the NHS's illustration, and expected to roughly double over the following week. Population averages, not a description of any one pregnancy.
The head has started to uncurl. Arms are lengthening faster than legs, because the upper body grows first. Around this point the embryo starts to be called a foetus.
What care usually happens around now

The booking appointment usually happens between weeks 8 and 12 in the UK, takes about an hour, and covers medical history, blood pressure, a urine sample, and blood tests. Screening for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis is offered, as are screening choices to discuss for later in pregnancy.

A dating scan is offered somewhere between weeks 8 and 14. NICHD describes a similar first-visit pattern in the US, with the schedule set by the clinician rather than a national timetable — so the shape is shared even when the dates are not.
This week's tip

Write your questions down before the booking appointment and take the list in with you. An hour sounds long and disappears fast, and the questions people forget are always the ones they were embarrassed to ask. If a previous pregnancy ended in loss, put that at the top of the list — it changes the care that is offered.
When to see a doctor
Contact a midwife or GP for any bleeding, severe or one-sided pain, an inability to keep fluids down, or a fever. If you feel unable to cope, say that too.
What happens at the first pregnancy appointment
explains the visit itself.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, pain in the tip of your shoulder, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
What actually happens at a booking appointment?
Medical history, blood pressure, urine, blood tests, and a conversation about screening choices and where you might give birth.
Pregnancy warning signs
is worth reading before you go, so you know what to ask about.
I am crying at everything. Is that hormones?
Mood changes are extremely common in the first trimester, and that does not make them trivial.
Week 9
is the week hormone levels usually peak. Tell your midwife how you are feeling — it is a routine question, not a difficult one.

en.title: Week 9 of Pregnancy: What to Expect
en.excerpt: Week 9 is when pregnancy hormone levels usually peak, which is why it is often the hardest week of the first trimester.

children.text: Week 9 is, for a lot of women, the low point. Pregnancy hormone levels peak around now, and everything they cause peaks with them. It does get better, and knowing that is most of what week 9 has to offer.
Your body this week

Human chorionic gonadotrophin has been roughly doubling every two to three days, and the NHS puts its peak at around week 9. Oestrogen and progesterone are high too, and together they are increasing the blood supply to the womb.

Breasts are bigger and the waist may be thickening a little, though nothing looks obviously pregnant yet. Some women describe this stretch as an emotional rollercoaster, which is a description rather than a diagnosis, and it is one the NHS repeats because it is so widely reported.
Rest is the only intervention on offer for most of it, and accepting help is worth more this week than at any other point in the first trimester.
What you may notice

Extreme tiredness, sickness, mood swings, a metallic taste, sore breasts, headaches, food likes and dislikes, a sharper sense of smell, a white milky discharge, light spotting, cramping, darker skin patches, and bloating.

Eating little and often keeps blood sugar steadier, which for some women reduces nausea. The NHS suggests simple things — a boiled egg with toast, hummus with carrot sticks, pitta with grated cheese — because complicated food is exactly what nobody manages in week 9.
If you cannot keep fluids down, contact a midwife or doctor. That is the line, and it is not a high one.
Your baby this week
Around week 9, the length quoted is about 22mm from head to bottom, which the NHS compares to a strawberry. It is a population figure and nothing about your own scan has to match it.

The face is more recognisable, with eyes now covered by eyelids, a mouth and a tongue with early taste buds. Hands and feet are forming, though fingers and toes are still only grooves. The heart, brain, lungs, kidneys and gut are all developing, and bones are beginning to form.
What care usually happens around now

Nothing routine, unless your booking appointment falls this week. Screening choices for later in pregnancy are usually discussed at that visit, and the dating scan follows somewhere between weeks 8 and 14 in the UK. Timetables vary between countries.
This week's tip

Put three snacks you can eat without cooking somewhere you will see them — the desk, the bag, the bedside. Week 9 is not the week to plan meals. It is the week to remove every step between being hungry and eating, because an empty stomach makes the nausea worse and the tiredness longer.
When to see a doctor
Contact a midwife or GP if you cannot keep fluids down, if you are losing weight, if you are passing very little urine, or if you feel faint on standing. Any bleeding should be reported.
Pregnancy warning signs
covers the full set.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if you have heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided tummy pain, pain in the tip of your shoulder, a severe headache with vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a fever, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or a seizure. Femio cannot assess a pregnancy.
Frequently asked questions
When will I stop feeling like this?
Many women improve after the first trimester ends at week 12, though some feel better earlier and some later.
Week 10
and
week 8
sit either side of the peak.
Is being this tired normal?

Extreme tiredness is one of the most reported first-trimester symptoms. It is still worth mentioning at your next appointment, because tiredness has causes other than pregnancy and a blood test is easy.

en.title: Can I Fast in Ramadan While Pregnant?
en.excerpt: What the research says about fasting in Ramadan during pregnancy, who should talk to a clinician first, and the warning signs that mean stop fasting and get help.

children.text: There is no single answer for every pregnant woman. A 2018 review of 22 studies found no clear link between fasting in Ramadan and lower birth weight or preterm birth, but the evidence has gaps, especially for women with diabetes. Whether fasting suits you is a decision to make with your clinician, and your religious scholar can advise on the faith side.
This is health information to help you learn and plan. It is not a substitute for your own clinician. If you notice a warning sign, get care now.
What does the research say?

The 2018 review pooled 22 studies covering 31,374 pregnancies. The difference in birth weight between fasting and non-fasting mothers was very small. Preterm birth was about the same in both groups (odds ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.37). The authors said the evidence on other outcomes was not sufficient. No included study reported deaths around birth.
Glazier et al. 2018

A 2023 review written for obstetricians reached similar conclusions on birth weight and preterm birth. It found that fasting is mainly linked with tiredness and dehydration, with a small drop in weight gain. It also noted conflicting data on gestational diabetes, not enough data on high blood pressure in pregnancy, and possible changes in some fetal tests.
Shahawy et al. 2023
What this means:
On average, the studies are reassuring. They cannot predict what will happen in your pregnancy. Some questions are still open.
Who should talk to a clinician before deciding?
These situations are not rules. They are reasons to plan with your clinician before you decide.
Gestational diabetes

(diabetes that first appears in pregnancy), especially if you take any medicine to lower blood sugar. A 2022 review found only five small studies of fasting in pregnancy. Most of them looked at women with gestational diabetes.
Kumar and Diamond 2022
and
NHS: gestational diabetes
Pre-eclampsia or high blood pressure in pregnancy.
The NHS lists high blood pressure as an early sign of pre-eclampsia, a pregnancy complication.
NHS: pre-eclampsia
Severe or repeated vomiting.
The NHS says to tell your midwife or doctor if you are being sick often and cannot keep food down, because of the risk of dehydration.
NHS: severe vomiting in pregnancy
Questions to bring to your appointment:
Does my health history or this pregnancy make fasting a concern for me?
If I fast, when and how often should I check my blood sugar?
Which symptoms mean I should stop fasting and call you?
Who do I contact outside clinic hours?
My glucose screening test may fall during Ramadan. What should I do? The NHS says the glucose test needs no food or drink for 8 to 10 hours, so tell your team about any fasting.
NHS: gestational diabetes
If you and your clinician decide to fast
This is a shared plan. Take these points to your team:
Meals:
Ask a dietitian or your clinician what suhoor (the pre-dawn meal) and iftar (the sunset meal) should look like for you.
Fluids:
Ask how much fluid is right for you between sunset and dawn. Signs of dehydration are in the box below.
Records:
Note any blood sugar readings your team asks for, and any symptoms. Bring the notes to appointments.
Gestational diabetes and Ramadan

Gestational diabetes usually causes no symptoms. Most cases are found by screening blood tests. Some women notice high blood sugar signs: increased thirst, needing to pee more often, a dry mouth, tiredness, blurred eyesight, or genital itching. Many of these are common in pregnancy anyway.
NHS: gestational diabetes

Low blood sugar (a hypo) is one of the main concerns. A hypo is usually a blood sugar below 4 mmol/L. Its signs include hunger, dizziness, feeling anxious or irritable, sweating, shaking, tingling lips, a racing heartbeat, tiredness, blurred vision, and confusion.
NHS: low blood sugar
A 2022 review of five small studies found lower average blood sugar and more frequent low blood sugar during fasting. It said the data on serious low blood sugar needing hospital care were limited.
Kumar and Diamond 2022

The same 2022 review says the current medical recommendation is against Ramadan fasting for pregnant women with diabetes. Ask your diabetes and maternity team which guidance they follow for you before Ramadan begins.
When to see a doctor
Contact your midwife or doctor before Ramadan if you are unsure whether fasting is safe for you. Contact them if you are worried about any symptom.
NHS: gestational diabetes
Seek care now:
Stop fasting and get medical help now if you have any of these:  - Your baby moves less than usual, or the movements stop.
RCOG guideline 57
- Vaginal bleeding, or fluid leaking from the vagina.
CDC
- Severe belly pain that does not go away.
CDC
- You are less than 37 weeks pregnant and have regular tightening of the womb, or think you might be in labour.
NHS: signs that labour has begun
- Dizziness or fainting.
CDC
- Trouble breathing, chest pain, or a fast-beating heart.
CDC
- A severe headache that does not go away, vision changes or flashing lights, pain below your ribs, or sudden swelling of your face, hands or feet.
NHS: pre-eclampsia
- Low blood sugar symptoms with confusion, a seizure or fit, or passing out.
NHS: low blood sugar
- Signs of dehydration: dark yellow or strong-smelling pee, peeing much less, dizziness when you stand that does not go away, or unusual tiredness.
NHS: dehydration
- Vomiting so that you cannot keep food or fluids down for 24 hours, or no pee for more than 8 hours.
NHS: vomiting and morning sickness
- New or worse thirst, frequent peeing, dry mouth, or blurred eyesight with high blood sugar.
NHS: gestational diabetes

If you are confused, cannot stay awake, have a seizure, or cannot reach your team, contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department. Do not wait for Femio or another online service to respond.
Femio cannot assess an emergency. Read more about
pregnancy warning signs that need urgent care
. See how Femio's health content is checked on the
clinician review page
and the
editorial policy
. Terms like "hypo" are explained in the
glossary
. If you feel unsafe, use the
help-now page
Frequently asked questions
Does fasting harm the baby?

The reviews did not find a clear effect on birth weight or preterm birth. They did not have enough data on every outcome, including deaths around birth. Talk to your clinician about your own pregnancy.
Do I have to fast?
Egypt's Dar al-Ifta says a woman who is unable to fast because of pregnancy or nursing may refrain from fasting, and should make up the missed days when she is able.
Dar al-Ifta
Your religious scholar can advise on the religious side. Your clinician can advise on the medical side.
Can I fast if I have gestational diabetes?

That is a decision to make with your clinician. A 2022 review states that the current medical recommendation is against Ramadan fasting for pregnant women with diabetes. Your team can weigh that against your blood sugar readings and your health.
Kumar and Diamond 2022
What if I feel unwell during the day?
Check the box above. If any sign appears, stop fasting and get medical help now.

en.title: Safer Sleep for Your Baby
en.excerpt: What safer sleep guidance covers, where national guidance agrees, where it differs on bed sharing, and how to find the advice that applies where you live.

children.text: Safer sleep guidance around the world agrees on the core: babies sleep on their backs, on a firm flat surface, in their own clear sleep space, in the same room as an adult for the early months. Countries differ on bed sharing, and that difference is real rather than a translation problem, so this page describes both positions and points you to the advice where you live. This is health information for learning and it is not medical advice about your baby. Anything about your own baby's sleep, breathing or health belongs with a health visitor, paediatrician or emergency service.
What the guidance is for

Sudden infant death syndrome, or SIDS, is the sudden unexplained death of an apparently well baby. CDC groups it with other sudden unexpected infant deaths, including deaths from accidental suffocation and strangulation in bed.
Nothing removes the risk entirely, and no parent causes it by being tired. Safer sleep guidance exists because a small number of changes to where and how a baby sleeps are linked with lower risk.
NHS guidance says the risk is highest in the first six months, that it can affect babies up to a year old, and that it can happen at any sleep, day or night.
Where guidance agrees
On the back, for every sleep, naps included. NHS and AAP guidance both say back sleeping, and both say to move a baby onto their back if they roll before they can roll both ways on their own.
On a firm, flat surface, with a fitted sheet and nothing else. No pillows, duvets, cot bumpers, loose blankets, soft toys, pods or nests.

In the same room as an adult for the first six months, in the baby's own cot, crib or Moses basket. Never on a sofa or armchair with a baby, which both bodies name as one of the most dangerous places to fall asleep together.
Not too hot. NHS guidance suggests a room around 16C to 20C, checking the baby's chest or the back of the neck rather than hands and feet, and taking hats and extra layers off indoors.

No smoking in pregnancy or around the baby, and nobody smoking in the same room. Where a baby falls asleep in a car seat, pram, swing or sling, both bodies advise moving them to a flat surface when you can.
Premature babies are a special case. NHS guidance says to follow safer sleep advice for a year from the original due date rather than the birth date.
Where guidance differs, and how to handle it
Bed sharing is the split. AAP does not recommend bed sharing at any point in the first year, and advises room sharing without it.

NHS guidance also says the safest place is a separate cot or Moses basket, and then gives advice on sharing a bed more safely, because many families do it whether or not it is recommended. That advice includes a firm flat mattress, the baby on their back, pillows and blankets kept away from the baby, no swaddling, no other children or pets in the bed, and never leaving the baby alone in an adult bed.

Both agree on when bed sharing is most dangerous. NHS guidance says never share a bed if you or a partner smoke, have drunk alcohol, or have taken drugs or medicine that makes you drowsy, and not if the baby was born before 37 weeks or weighed under 2.5kg at birth.

Follow the guidance published where you live, and tell your midwife or health visitor honestly how your baby actually sleeps. A plan built on what really happens at four in the morning is safer than one built on what should happen.
Other things linked with lower risk
NHS guidance names breastfeeding, offering a dummy for sleep, and keeping a baby up to date with routine vaccinations as things associated with lower SIDS risk.
Your baby's first checks and vaccinations
covers what is usually offered and when.
None of these are a substitute for the sleep position and the sleep space, which are the parts with the strongest evidence behind them.
When exhaustion is the real problem

Most unplanned bed sharing happens because a parent falls asleep feeding, not because anyone decided to. Knowing that in advance is why guidance is worth reading before the hard night rather than during it.
If you are so tired that you fall asleep wherever you sit, that is a reason to ask for help. See
sleep and exhaustion after birth
, and
newborn crying
for the nights that will not end.
When to see a doctor
Seek urgent care for any sign in the box below, at any hour. Sleep advice never overrides a baby who looks unwell.

Ask a health visitor or doctor about sleep if your baby will only sleep upright, if breathing during sleep worries you, or if your baby was born early or has a health condition and you are unsure which advice applies. See
your newborn in the first two weeks
for what is usual, and
newborn warning signs
for what is not.
Seek care now:

Contact your local emergency services or go to your nearest emergency department if a baby under three months old has a temperature of 38C or higher, is breathing fast, working hard to breathe or grunting, has blue, grey, pale or mottled skin, is floppy, is difficult to wake, is refusing feeds, has far fewer wet nappies or none in the past 12 hours, has a bulging or sunken soft spot on the head, has a rash that does not fade when you press it, or has a fit. Femio cannot assess a baby.
Frequently asked questions
What if my baby rolls onto their front?
Guidance is to always place a baby on their back, and to turn them back until they can roll both ways by themselves. Keep the cot clear of anything they could roll into.
Is bed sharing banned?

Guidance differs. AAP advises against bed sharing; NHS advice names a separate cot as safest and then explains how to share a bed more safely. Both agree it is dangerous after alcohol, drugs or drowsy medicine, if anyone smokes, and never on a sofa or armchair.
Are sleep positioners, pods and nests safe?
Guidance advises against anything in the cot that could cover a baby's face, and against products not designed and approved for infant sleep.
Can a baby choke on their back?
Guidance is clear that back sleeping is advised for all babies, including babies who bring up milk. Ask a paediatrician if your baby has a condition that makes you unsure.

en.title: Sex After Birth: What to Expect
en.excerpt: When sex after birth is usually possible, why it often hurts at first, what helps with dryness and scar pain, and what is worth reporting.

children.text: There is no fixed date when sex after birth becomes allowed. Most guidance suggests waiting until bleeding has stopped and any stitches or wounds have healed, and beyond that it is about whether you want to and whether it is comfortable. Dryness, tightness and scar pain are extremely common at first, and there are things that help. This is health information for planning, not a substitute for advice from your own clinician.
The six-week rule is not a rule
Six weeks is the usual figure because it lines up with the postnatal check, not because something changes on that day. Some people feel ready earlier and many feel ready much later.
Waiting until bleeding has stopped and wounds have healed lowers the chance of infection and discomfort. Beyond that, readiness is yours to judge — including emotionally.
Pregnancy is possible before your first period, so the contraception conversation comes before the sex one. See
contraception after birth
Why it often hurts at first
Dryness.
Oestrogen is low after birth, and lower still while breastfeeding, which makes the vaginal tissue thinner and drier. This is the single most common cause of pain, and it is temporary.
Scar tissue.
A perineal tear, an episiotomy, or a caesarean scar can feel tight or tender for months. See
wound healing after birth
Pelvic floor tension.
Muscles often tighten protectively after birth, which can make penetration painful. This responds well to pelvic health physiotherapy — see
your pelvic floor after birth
Exhaustion and touch fatigue.
Being held, fed from and climbed on all day genuinely reduces the appetite for more touch. That is not a relationship problem in itself.
What helps
Lubricant, generously.
A water-based lubricant is the most useful single item. Use more than seems necessary.
Time and unhurried arousal.
Rushing makes tension worse.
Positions you control,
so depth and speed are yours to set.
Stopping when it hurts,
rather than pushing through. Pushing through pain teaches the body to brace.
Starting with things other than penetration,
with no obligation for it to lead anywhere.
Saying out loud what you are worried about.
Fear of pain causes tension, which causes pain.
If dryness is severe or is not improving, ask your clinician. There are options they can discuss with you, including ones suitable while breastfeeding.
Desire, and the honest version

Low desire in the months after birth is common and has plenty of reasons: hormones, exhaustion, pain, body changes, the mental load, and having no time alone in your own head. Feeding also lowers oestrogen, which affects desire for some people.
Desire usually returns as sleep improves and pain settles. It rarely returns on a schedule, and comparing timelines with anyone else is not useful.
If low mood or anxiety is part of the picture, that matters too — read
your mood after birth
Talking about it with a partner
The gap between two people's readiness is normal and is worth naming rather than avoiding. Say what you do want, not only what you do not.
Closeness without sex is not a holding pattern. It is often what makes sex easier later.
If a partner is pressuring you, that is not a bedroom problem to solve alone. Tell a clinician you trust.
What is worth reporting
Pain that continues beyond the first few attempts, or that is severe.
Bleeding after sex.
A feeling of tearing, or a scar that catches.
Being unable to tolerate penetration at all.
Leaking urine during sex.
Ongoing dryness that lubricant does not solve.
NICE's postnatal guidance
expects these to be asked about after birth, and they are treatable. Raise them at
your six-week check
if not before.
When to see a doctor

Contact your doctor, midwife or a women's health service for pain that persists or is severe, bleeding after sex, an uncomfortable scar, leaking during sex, or dryness that is not helped by lubricant. Ask about a pelvic health physiotherapy referral, which is often the most useful step for pain.
Seek urgent care for heavy bleeding, severe pain, or a wound that seems to have opened.
Frequently asked questions
How long should I wait before sex after birth?
Most guidance suggests waiting until bleeding has stopped and any wounds have healed. After that, it depends on comfort and on whether you want to.
Why is it so dry?
Oestrogen is low after birth and lower while breastfeeding, which thins and dries the vaginal tissue. Lubricant helps, and it improves with time.
Is pain during sex after birth normal?
Discomfort at first is common. Pain that continues or is severe is not something to accept, and it responds to help.
Can I get pregnant if my periods have not returned?
Yes. Ovulation happens before the first period, so pregnancy is possible before any bleeding.
My desire has disappeared. Will it come back?
Usually, as sleep, pain and hormones settle. If low mood is part of it, that is worth raising with a clinician.

en.title: Your Six-Week Check After Birth
en.excerpt: What the postnatal check is for, what usually happens, and how to make sure your own health is on the agenda rather than only the baby's.

children.text: The postnatal check is an appointment about you, roughly six weeks after the birth, separate from the baby's checks. It usually covers how you are recovering physically, how you are feeling, feeding, bleeding, bladder and bowel, contraception, and any problems from the birth. It is often short, so going in with a written list changes what you get out of it. This page helps you prepare, and it is not a substitute for the appointment itself.
Why it exists
The weeks after birth are when serious problems can appear and be missed, because attention has moved to the baby.
ACOG
argues for postnatal care as an ongoing process rather than a single visit, with earlier contact for people who need it.
WHO's postnatal guidance
also sets out multiple contacts across the first six weeks, not one appointment at the end of them.
So the six-week check is a backstop, not the only chance. Anything worrying before then deserves a call at the time.
What usually happens
The details vary by country and service, and commonly include:
How you are feeling emotionally, sometimes with a short questionnaire.
Bleeding, and whether periods have returned.
Wound or scar healing, and pain.
Bladder and bowel control.
Feeding, and any pain with it.
Contraception and plans for future pregnancies.
Blood pressure, especially if it was raised in pregnancy.
Any blood tests you were told you would need, such as iron or thyroid, or a repeat glucose test if you had gestational diabetes.
Vaccinations and cervical screening if either is due.
An examination is not always part of it and is not always necessary. Ask if you want something looked at.
What to raise, even if nobody asks
Bring these up yourself. They are the most commonly missed:
Mood.
Say the true version, not the polite one. See
your mood after birth
Leaking urine, wind or stool, or a heavy dragging feeling.
Ask about a pelvic health physiotherapy referral — see
your pelvic floor after birth
Pain during sex,
or fear of it.
Scar or perineal pain
that is not settling.
Exhaustion
that feels beyond broken sleep, especially with breathlessness or dizziness.
The birth itself,
if it was frightening or you have unanswered questions. You can ask for a debrief with the maternity service.
Contraception,
even if sex feels remote — see
contraception after birth
NICE's postnatal guidance
lists physical and emotional recovery, bladder and bowel function, and contraception among the things postnatal care should cover, so none of this is off-topic.
How to prepare in five minutes
Write three things you most want answered, in order, and say them at the start. Appointments drift, and the last item on a list often does not get reached.
Bring notes on symptoms, bleeding, mood and sleep. If you have logged them in Femio, bring that. A record of three bad weeks is more persuasive than trying to remember a bad Tuesday.
Take someone with you if you can, especially for a difficult conversation. And arrange the appointment for a time when the baby is usually settled, or take someone who can hold them.
If the appointment does not cover you
Some checks turn into a baby appointment with a question about you at the end. If that happens, say plainly: "I have something about my own health I need to discuss."
If you do not get anywhere, ask for a separate appointment for yourself. That is a reasonable request, and it is what the check is meant to be.
After six weeks
Six weeks is not the end of recovery. Pelvic floor strength, scar comfort, sleep, mood and cycles can all take months longer, and problems that appear later are still postnatal problems.
The first six weeks after birth
describes the timeline, and
postpartum warning signs
lists what should not wait for any appointment.
When to see a doctor

Do not wait for the six-week check for bleeding that is getting heavier, a wound that is more painful or red, a fever, calf pain or swelling, a severe headache, low mood lasting beyond two weeks, or any thought of harming yourself or your baby. Seek urgent care for the emergency signs in the warning-signs guide, and use Femio's global
Need help now
page if you feel unable to stay safe.
Ask for an earlier appointment if you had a complicated birth, raised blood pressure, gestational diabetes, heavy blood loss, or a previous mental health condition.
Frequently asked questions
Is the six-week check about me or the baby?
It is meant to be about you. The baby usually has separate checks, though services sometimes combine them.
Will I be examined?
Not always, and not necessarily. Ask if there is something you want looked at.
What if I am not offered a check?
Ask for one. Contact your doctor's surgery or your postnatal service and say you would like your postnatal appointment.
Can I bring up something months later?
Yes. Postnatal problems do not stop at six weeks, and it is not too late to raise them.
What should I take with me?
Your three main questions, notes on symptoms and mood, your maternity notes if you have them, and a list of any medicines you take.

en.title: Sleep and Exhaustion After Birth
en.excerpt: Why exhaustion after birth is more than broken sleep, what actually helps, and when tiredness is a symptom rather than a stage.

children.text: Exhaustion after birth is not only broken sleep. A body that has just been through pregnancy and birth is repairing, often short of iron, feeding a baby around the clock, and running on sleep chopped into pieces. Most of it improves as feeds spread out, and some tiredness is a symptom worth checking rather than a stage to endure. This is health information for planning, not a substitute for advice from your own clinician.
Why it is this heavy
Newborns feed often, day and night, because their stomachs are small. Sleep in short blocks is not a sign you are doing anything wrong.
Blood loss at birth can leave iron low, which causes tiredness, breathlessness and dizziness that no nap fixes. Thyroid changes after birth can also cause exhaustion.
Pain, wound healing, and the sheer mental load of being responsible for a new person all take energy.
What actually helps
Most sleep advice for new parents is unrealistic. These are the things that make a measurable difference:
Sleep when you can, not when it is night.
A 40-minute daytime sleep is real sleep.
Split the night if there are two of you.
One person takes the first stretch, the other the second, so each gets one unbroken block.
Lower the bar on everything else.
The house can wait. Nobody remembers a tidy kitchen from this period.
Accept every concrete offer of help,
and turn vague ones into concrete ones. "Bring dinner Thursday" is a better answer than "thanks, we are fine".
Keep night feeds boring.
Low light, little talking, back down. This is for you as much as the baby.
Get outside in daylight once a day
if you can. It helps how the day feels, even when it does not add hours.

Sleeping arrangements are a safety question as well as a tiredness one, and safer-sleep advice differs between countries. Ask your midwife or health visitor about the guidance where you live rather than following what you read online.
When tiredness is a symptom
Some exhaustion is not about sleep at all. Tell a clinician if you have:
Breathlessness climbing stairs, a racing heart, or dizziness.
Very pale skin, or lips and nail beds that look washed out.
Tiredness that is getting worse rather than better after the early weeks.
Feeling cold all the time, hair falling out heavily, or unexplained weight change.
Sleeping and waking unrefreshed for weeks.
Being unable to sleep even when the baby sleeps.
Low iron after a heavy blood loss is common and treatable, and a blood test settles it.
Heavy periods and iron-deficiency anaemia
explains what low iron feels like.
Thyroid problems can appear in the months after birth and cause exhaustion, and
ACOG's postpartum care guidance
frames the postnatal period as ongoing care rather than one visit, which is the point at which these things get picked up.
Exhaustion and mood

Not sleeping and low mood feed each other, and they are hard to pull apart from the inside. One useful signal: being unable to sleep when the baby is asleep, night after night, points towards mood or anxiety rather than sleep deprivation alone.
If you are lying awake checking the baby is breathing, or dread the night, read
your mood after birth
. That is worth raising with a clinician.
Feeding and sleep
Feeding often at night is normal in the early weeks, however you feed. Bottle feeding does not reliably buy longer nights, though it does make it easier for someone else to take a feed.
Babies do not sleep on a schedule at this age and cannot be trained to at this age. Advice promising otherwise usually costs money and delivers guilt.
Going back to work, and the second wave
Many people find the tiredness peaks again around returning to work, when the day gets longer but the nights do not shorten. Plan for that rather than being surprised by it.
NICE's postnatal guidance
expects wellbeing to be asked about at postnatal contacts, so use them. Bring it up at
your six-week check
even if it feels like complaining about something ordinary.
What Femio can hold

Logging sleep, mood and energy for a week gives you a real picture instead of an impression. "Longest stretch was 90 minutes, five nights running, and I am breathless on the stairs" is a sentence that gets a blood test.
Femio does not diagnose anaemia, thyroid problems or anything else. It holds what you noticed so someone qualified can act on it. See also
the first six weeks after birth
When to see a doctor

Contact your doctor or postnatal service for tiredness with breathlessness, palpitations, dizziness or paleness, for exhaustion that is worsening after the early weeks, or for being unable to sleep even when the baby does. Seek urgent care for chest pain, severe breathlessness, or fainting.
Ask for a blood test if you had heavy bleeding at birth and still feel wiped out weeks later. It is a reasonable request.
Frequently asked questions
How long does newborn exhaustion last?
Feeds usually spread out over the first months, and most people notice real improvement in the second half of the first year.
Is it normal to feel breathless from tiredness?
Breathlessness is not just tiredness. It needs checking, especially after heavy bleeding.
Should I nap during the day?
Yes, if you can. Short daytime sleep counts and is worth taking over chores.
Can I train a newborn to sleep through?
No. Frequent feeding at this age is normal, and approaches that promise otherwise are not appropriate for newborns.
Why am I awake even when the baby is asleep?
That pattern points towards anxiety or low mood rather than sleep deprivation alone, and it is worth telling a clinician.

en.title: Thyroid Conditions and Trying to Conceive
en.excerpt: Why a thyroid condition is worth reviewing before you conceive rather than after, what usually gets checked, and what changes as soon as a test is positive.

children.text: If you have a thyroid condition and are trying to conceive, the useful step is a review
before

a positive test rather than after one. Thyroid needs change early in pregnancy — often within the first weeks, before a first appointment would normally happen — so being set up in advance is worth more than reacting later. This page explains what usually gets checked and what changes, and it is not a substitute for the clinician who manages your thyroid.
Do not change any medicine on your own because of anything here.
Why the timing matters so much
In early pregnancy a baby depends entirely on the mother's thyroid hormone until its own gland develops, and the demand on the mother's thyroid rises quickly.
The American Thyroid Association

describes that increase beginning very early — often before a woman has seen anyone about the pregnancy. That is the whole argument for a preconception review: the window where it matters most opens before the appointments do.
ACOG
similarly frames thyroid conditions in pregnancy as something managed with a clinician throughout, rather than checked once.
What usually gets reviewed before you start
Your current test results
, and how recently they were taken.
Your medicine
, and whether the dose is right for where you are now. Adjustments in pregnancy are common and are your prescriber's decision — this page gives no doses and no thresholds.
Antibody status
, if it is relevant to you and has not been checked.
Other medicines and supplements
, since some affect how thyroid medicine is absorbed and the timing of when you take them can matter.
How often you will be retested
once you are pregnant, and who orders it.
Ask directly:
"If I get a positive test, what do you want me to do that day?"
A clear answer to that one question is most of what a preconception review is for.
The
preconception appointment
guide covers the rest of what belongs in that visit.
What changes the day a test is positive
Usually two things: your medicine may need reviewing quickly, and your testing becomes more frequent. Many clinicians give people a plan in advance precisely so nothing waits on an appointment slot.

If you were not given one, contact whoever manages your thyroid as soon as you have a positive test. Say that you are pregnant and that you take thyroid medicine — that sentence usually moves the appointment.
Do not stop taking your medicine because you are pregnant. That is a common and understandable fear, and it is the opposite of what guidance describes.
Thyroid problems and conceiving

Thyroid conditions can affect cycles, and irregular or absent periods are one of the ways an untreated problem shows up. That is one reason thyroid tests are part of a standard fertility assessment — see
what a fertility assessment involves
If you have a thyroid condition and have been trying without success, mention it explicitly when you ask for help, and bring your recent results. Read
when to seek fertility help
for the timing.
Being managed for a thyroid condition is not itself a reason to expect difficulty. It is a reason to have the review.
What to keep track of

Your own results, with dates. Your current medicine and any changes to it. Symptoms that are new or changing — tiredness, weight change, feeling cold or hot, palpitations, hair changes — with when they started.
Femio can hold that record and show it as a timeline. It does
not

interpret a result: a number sits with the laboratory's own reference range and nothing else, because reading it against a target is a clinical judgement, and the targets differ between guidelines and between stages of pregnancy.
When to see a doctor

Contact the clinician who manages your thyroid before you start trying, and again as soon as a pregnancy test is positive. Contact them sooner if you have new palpitations, unusual weight change, feeling much hotter or colder than usual, or worsening tiredness. Seek prompt care for chest pain, a very fast heartbeat, severe breathlessness, or confusion.
If your periods are irregular or absent and your thyroid has not been checked recently, ask for it as part of the same conversation.
Frequently asked questions
Should I get my thyroid checked before trying?
If you have a known thyroid condition, yes — a review before conception is the point of this page. If you do not, thyroid tests are part of a standard fertility assessment when one is offered.
Will my medicine change in pregnancy?
Requirements often change early, and adjustments are common. Your prescriber decides them; nothing on this page names a dose.
Should I stop my thyroid medicine when I get pregnant?
No. Contact your prescriber promptly, and do not stop on your own.
Can a thyroid problem stop me conceiving?
It can affect cycles, which is one reason thyroid tests are part of a standard assessment. Being managed for one is not itself a reason to expect difficulty.
Can Femio tell me if my result is normal?
No. It shows your results with the laboratory's own reference range and no verdict, because interpreting them is a clinical judgement and the targets differ between guidelines.

en.title: How Should You Track Perimenopause Symptoms?
en.excerpt: Learn how to track period changes, hot flushes, sleep, mood, and daily impact during perimenopause without treating app estimates as medical conclusions.

children.text: Track the changes that matter most to you, such as period dates, flow, hot flushes, sleep, mood, headaches, or vaginal and bladder symptoms. Add a short note about daily impact. A simple record can support a clinical conversation, but it cannot confirm perimenopause or rule out another cause.
Choose a small set you can record consistently rather than trying to track everything.
Start with your main question
Ask what you want the record to help with. You may want to understand changing periods, explain night sweats, compare sleep and mood, or prepare to discuss care.
Pick three to six items linked to that goal. You can change them later. Tracking should serve you, not become another burden.
The main
perimenopause guide
explains the life stage and common changes.
How should you record periods?
Record:
The first and last day of bleeding.
Light, medium, or heavy flow.
Spotting between periods.
Bleeding after sex.
Clots, flooding, or leaks.
Pain and dizziness.
Cycles may become closer together, farther apart, or less predictable. Use the same rule for Day 1 each time. The guide to
tracking your menstrual cycle
explains a consistent method.
Do not assume every bleeding change is due to perimenopause. Read the
heavy-period guide
when flow affects daily life.
Which body symptoms may be useful to track?
The
NHS symptom guide
lists a wide range of possible changes. You might record:
Hot flushes and night sweats.
Sleep quality and waking.
Headaches or migraine changes.
Joint or muscle aches.
Palpitations, or a fast and noticeable heartbeat.
Vaginal dryness or pain during sex.
Bladder urgency or repeated urine infections.
Skin or hair changes.
Record timing, strength, duration, and effect. “Woke three times with sweats and felt too tired to drive” is more useful than “bad night.”
How should you track mood and thinking changes?
You may notice low mood, anxiety, irritability, poor focus, or memory concerns. Use neutral words and one simple scale. Add whether the change affected work, relationships, sleep, or self-care.
Mood symptoms can have many causes and may overlap with depression, anxiety, thyroid issues, poor sleep, medicine effects, or major life stress. Tracking cannot decide the cause.
Seek help promptly if mood changes feel unsafe or you cannot manage daily life.
How long should you track?
A few weeks may show the effect of frequent symptoms. Several months may better show changing cycles. Do not delay care just to collect more data.
Review the record at a set interval, such as once a week. Daily review can make normal variation feel more alarming. Look for patterns without forcing one.
How do you make an appointment summary?
Keep the full record, but make a one-page summary with:
The dates covered.
Shortest and longest cycles.
Main bleeding changes.
The three symptoms with the greatest impact.
Changes from your earlier pattern.
Medicines and supplements.
What you want help with.
The
NICE menopause guidance
says care should be tailored to the person and adapted as symptoms change. Your summary should show what matters to you, not just a list of scores.
How can Femio estimates change?
Cycle estimates become less certain when periods vary. Femio should show a range rather than claim one exact future date. A “late” label cannot explain why a period did not arrive.
Pregnancy can still occur during perimenopause. A calendar cannot confirm whether ovulation happened.
These dates support conception planning and awareness. They are estimates, not a reliable way to avoid pregnancy.
What should you ask a clinician?
Ask which changes fit perimenopause and what else may need checking. Ask what each care option may help, what risks apply to you, and when the plan should be reviewed.
Read the
menopause overview
and
menopause care-options guide
before the visit if useful.
When to see a doctor

Book an appointment when symptoms affect sleep, work, mood, sex, or daily comfort. Seek advice for bleeding between periods, after sex, after 12 months without a period, or before age 45 when menopause-like changes begin.
Seek care now:

Get urgent medical help for very heavy bleeding with fainting, severe weakness, chest pain, or trouble breathing. Sudden severe pelvic or abdominal pain also needs prompt assessment. Contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department.
Frequently asked questions
Must I track every symptom?
No. Choose a small group linked to your main concern.
Can tracking confirm perimenopause?
No. It can show patterns and support a clinical discussion.
Should I wait months before seeking care?
No. Bring whatever record you have when symptoms worry you.
Are cycle predictions exact during perimenopause?
No. Changing cycles make calendar estimates less certain.
